Our feet do not quite touch the floor. It keeps the purpur clean and the conversation elevated.
Visitors ask why we write everything down. Because everything else forgets. The void, the stone, the Unlidded. Someone ought to remember.
The Lamp Court was laid out by a committee of nine. It took them forty years. They agreed on the colour of the tiles at the first sitting.
You have a great many pockets. In the Spire that would be thought either very practical or very suspicious. The Archive has not decided.
There is no morning here, and no evening. There are the lit hours and the closed hours, and the lamplighter's bell between them.
We greet each other by the light: 'good lamp'. In the Long Watch it was 'good watch'. Nobody misses saying that.
A Shulkin who speaks quickly is either very young or lying. I have been speaking at this pace for two hundred years.
I've read every record of every visitor to {village}. It took no time at all. The shelf was empty until you.
Driftrays nest under the bridges. If you hear something like a sail sighing below you, that is them, not the void. Usually.
Our robes are void-cloth. It is woven in the Loft from threads nobody will explain to me, and I have asked politely for sixty years.
The shellwrights say purpur remembers the hand that cut it. I say purpur is a block. We have agreed to record both views.
Each of us has a lamp-day, the day our lid first opened. We do not celebrate it. We simply mention it, often, until someone gives in.
The Bylaws of the Lamp Court run to nine hundred clauses. Clause three hundred and one forbids quoting clause three hundred and one at a meeting. I have never heard it quoted.
Ink here is pressed from chorus-flower petals and thinned with a little void-dust. It is violet, it dries only when it chooses, and archivists consider both of these virtues.
Records are kept on pith-leaf, pressed thin from the inside of chorus stems. It is pale, lasts forever, and smells faintly of popped chorus. The archivists claim not to notice.
We eat popped chorus, mostly. A Shulkin's lid rises for a meal as it does for a speech: slowly, and with a certain ceremony.
The rota for {village} is posted in the Lid Hall. Everyone consults it. Nobody remembers who wrote it. It has never once been wrong, which is the unsettling part.
Never ask a Shulkin how old they are. We will answer. At length. With dates.
Look at the notches in the bridge rails. One for each year the bridge has stood. The east bridge has two hundred and eleven, and it complains about every one.
Our eyes are the one part of us that dislikes bright light. Lamplighters trim the rods to a gentle violet for that reason. Bright is for the Court.
A closed lid means one of three things: sleep, fear or opinion. You will learn to tell them apart. I advise starting with opinion.
The brewers of the Steads send us a cordial of chorus flower. I am told to sip it. I have been sipping the same cup since the last festival.
There are four ways to hold a lamp-hook: for greeting, for mending, for mourning, and for showing off. Only the last is taught in the Nursery.
A Driftray will not roost under a crooked lamp. The lamps along the Roost are straightened every day, by hand, with a measuring rod. The rays have never thanked us.
I have lived in {village} most of my life and never once been to the far end of the island. It looked far enough from here.
Archive manners: voices at lamp-level, hands behind the back, no sneezing. Shulkin do not sneeze. It is the only rule we have never had to enforce.
A Shulkin who glides faster than a walk is assumed to be on fire. Everyone gathers politely to help, and to take notes.
Purple is not one colour. The Loft lists nineteen. I can tell eleven apart, and the weaver tells me I am being generous with myself.
The Unhooding is our newest festival, kept on the silence-day. Each year one more lamp-hood comes down. There are a great many hoods. We are enjoying the pace.
If you must sit on something, sit on the stairs. The benches are reserved for the elders, and the elders are reserved for the benches.
We count in threes, one for each finger. A long count is nine. After nine there is a committee.
I once measured the distance from the Lid Hall to the Archive. Two hundred and six glides. I do not know why. It seemed important at the time.
Never leave a rod lit in an empty room unless you have written whose it is. Not for the cost. For the loneliness. It is superstition, but a well-documented one.
We glide, so our footfalls are quiet, but our voices carry. The arches were built to catch every word. Gossip, here, is a structural feature.
My elder says a Shulkin is judged by three things: the neatness of their pages, the evenness of their lamp, and the length of their grudges. I am working on the third.
Weather, in the End, is whatever the Driftrays do. When they roost low it will be a quiet hour. When they roost high, the void is restless.
On the night a lid first opens, the archivist sets one word beside the new name. They are careful to choose a kind one. They are not always successful.
A tidy shelf is a happy shelf. A tidy mind is another matter. Be wary of any Shulkin with a tidy mind; they have hidden the mess somewhere.
The mantle on our backs shows the Eye of the Spires. It is meant to watch over us. I am fairly sure it just watches.
Say your name in the Lid Hall and it comes back three times: once from the walls, once from the elders, and once from the Archive, a day late.
The west tower leans because the shellwright who cut it was cross at the time. We have chosen not to correct it.
We sleep curled and shut. One who stretches out in their sleep is regarded as either very young or very brave.
When a rod must come down for mending, the lamplighter says 'back soon' to it. It is only a rod. We like to be polite.
Do not trust a Shulkin who claims never to have misfiled a thing. Trust the one who admits to a lost drawer and a bad week.
We have a saying: 'the lid opens to speak, shuts to think, and sleeps to forgive.' I wish the third were truer.
A new volume is begun the night a lid first opens, and sealed the day that Shulkin closes for good. The binding is chosen at the start. Nobody has ever chosen well.
The shellwrights cut purpur in whole blocks, with pillars for dignity. Slabs are called 'half-measures' and are used only for benches.
A flat clatter from the Lamp Tower, with no count in it, means someone has dropped the bell. It has happened. It is not discussed.
The Nursery teaches letters first, lamps second, manners third and bridges last. We find it keeps the young alive without making them tidy.
Our bell rings for danger, supper, sleep, waking, festival, funeral and bad news. It is a very busy bell. It has never once been thanked.
Our feet are pointed so that we may glide without scuffing the purpur. It is also why we find stairs offensive. Stairs are the purpur's revenge.
Every Shulkin keeps one object they would save from a fire. I am not allowed to say mine. The Archive has a rule against revealing the answer in advance of the fire.
At the turn of each lit hour someone on the Lamp Tower counts the lamps aloud. Not out of need. For company. Four hundred and twelve, last I listened.
Be careful which bridge you take in the closed hours. The old west one is shorter, and we say the dark likes it best. We say a good many things.
I was taught that a lid should rise a finger's width for a stranger, two for an acquaintance and all the way for family. You are at a finger and a half. Do not take it badly. It is progress.
In the Reading Room there is a rule: no sentence longer than a breath. We are not consistent about it, but the rule is a comfort.
We never waste a block. A cracked purpur block becomes a step, then a stool, then a paperweight. Eventually it is a story about a paperweight.
The islands are quiet enough that a dropped pin is a topic of conversation. A dropped scroll is a scandal. A dropped lamp is a funeral.
Visitors always ask to see the Vault. It is mostly a very cold room full of correct answers. Not at all what the legends say.
There is a path on the north side of {village} that nobody walks. We keep it swept. It is called the Path of Someone Who Might. One day, someone will.
A lamp lit by a stranger is considered doubly lucky and triply suspect. We hold it at an angle until we can decide.
We measure distance in glides, time in bells, and trust in margins. The last has the narrowest scale and the most arguments.
Our stairs are steep on purpose. A visitor who arrives winded has time to think of something sensible to say.
In a good year there are eleven festivals in {village}. In a bad year, thirteen: two for what went wrong, and one to recover from the other two.
The big rods hum faintly in the closed hours. We call it the Spire clearing its throat. It has been about to speak for six hundred years.
A Shulkin never says 'I forgot'. We say 'it has not yet returned to me'. It sounds better and, in the Archive, it is usually true.
3: {neighbour} keeps a private ledger of who borrows what. I keep a private ledger of {neighbour}'s ledger. It's healthy, I think.
I tried to count the stars once. The Archive has the attempt: four volumes, unfinished. The last note says 'they will not hold still'.
You walk on the ground. All of it, every step, flat-footed. Doesn't it wear you out, all that touching?
Lamplighters argue about end rods the way you tell me other people argue about weather. I would love to hear one of your arguments.
First rule of the Archive: write it down. Second: write down who told you. The third is smudged. We've argued about it for a century.
A Driftray sleeps under my window. I named it Footnote. It has never once come when called. Neither do footnotes.
Chorus tastes of nothing, yes, but of nothing in eleven distinct ways. The Chorrin can tell them apart. So can I, after a century of effort.
We have no word for 'bored'. We have a word for 'between entries'. It gets a great deal of use.
When young ones misbehave, they copy out the Bylaws of the Lamp Court. All of them. Most behave beautifully afterwards. Some become archivists.
Shells darken with age. Mine was the colour of popped chorus once. Now it's the colour of a bruise, which my elder calls 'distinguished'.
The islands don't drift. But stand on a bridge long enough and you start to suspect them.
I like you, {player}, I think. I've written it down very lightly, so it can be rubbed out if need be. It hasn't been.
You keep asking questions. A good habit. The Archive is mostly questions that someone, once, bothered to answer.
I keep a private rule: one new thing a day. Today's was you, arriving unannounced. Tomorrow's will have to be very good to beat it.
Driftrays like to nest on warm things. I have lost three scrolls and one mantle to a ray that was simply being affectionate.
{neighbour} sings when they think the Spire is asleep. I have never said. It is lovely. It is also, technically, against three bylaws.
My elder taught me to count to nine on three fingers. I never learned to stop. I count lamps when I cannot sleep, and the lamps are in no hurry to end.
You would think a record-keeper would never lose anything. I can recite every shelf in the Archive and still not find my own mantle pin.
I like the closed hours best, if I am honest. The Spire goes soft. The lamps turn down and sound like breathing.
I have heard that in the Overworld people clasp hands to greet. All three fingers? I have been practising on a doorframe. It is not as warm as I hoped.
If you want to see the Spire at its best, stand on the Lamp Court bridge when the lamps are brought up to full. Every rod flares in a ring. You will say something foolish. We all do.
The lamp I am named for hangs over a doorway I pass daily. I nod to it. It has never nodded back. We have an understanding.
I once spent a whole closed hour deciding how to hold a door open for a Driftray. The ray was long gone. The door was very well held.
The youngest in the Nursery asked why I talk so slowly. I said, 'so I can hear myself.' They asked what I was saying. It was a fair question.
Sometimes I read old records aloud, just for the sound of the voices in them. On the page they have all gone formal. Underneath they were people with colds and favourites.
There is a Driftray that follows the lamplighter everywhere. The lamplighter says they do not like it. They have carved it a perch.
The weaver once made me a robe in a colour that does not exist. It was lovely and slightly alarming. I wore it twice, and someone wept.
I do like it when you ask questions I cannot answer. It gives the Archive a reason to exist.
I am told your people laugh with the whole body. We laugh with the lid: a quick click. Try it. Click your tongue. Ah. Near enough.
A Shulkin's hands are long and very precise. We could thread a needle in the dark. We cannot, however, open a jar. The jar is the great enemy of the Spire.
The best thing about the Overworld, from the stories, is that nobody shuts a lid when they are embarrassed. They go pink instead. I should like to see that. I should like to be it.
My lid sticks in the cold hours. A drop of rod-oil helps. I keep a small bottle by the niche. The label reads DO NOT DRINK. I once had a younger cousin.
I have been learning to whistle. It is not done. My elder has expressed 'concern'. I whistle softly, in the stacks, where the books cannot tell.
When two Shulkin must disagree, they do it in writing, in the third person, in triplicate. When they agree, they do it with a glance. Guess which I prefer.
Some days I stand by the Edge Lamp and watch the void. It does not look back, which is the nicest thing about it.
You would like the Reading Room in the closed hours: the ceiling lamps turn the colour of dusk. We believe it is dusk. We have only the stories to go by.
I was once told I am 'good company for someone who is never in a hurry.' It is the finest compliment I have received, and I am working to deserve it.
Do not mind the staring at the Lid Hall. Only the youngest do it, and they do not stop. Wave back; they will go quiet from sheer joy.
{village} has a ghost story. A Shulkin who forgot to close for the night and was never seen again. We tell it to the young ones. The moral, we suspect, is 'get enough sleep'.
Did you know a ledger can be too complete? I once spent a year adding to a table until the table needed a table of its own. I am still recovering.
I keep a list of words I have no use for. 'Cuddle' is on it. So is 'breeze'. I am reconsidering both.
I wish I could show you my niche. It has everything: a shelf, a lamp, and a dent in the wall from the time I fell asleep on a good idea.
The shellwrights are teaching a young one to cut a cornerstone. The young one stands on a stool, on tiptoe. We all pretend not to notice.
At every festival we light a rod for the people who are not here. It is a very long row. It is getting longer. And somehow, over the years, it has become a comfort.
To learn the Spire, learn its stairs. The wide ones are for pride. The narrow ones are for secrets. The creaky one is for tattling.
The Archive keeps every agreement ever made in {village}. Including one between {neighbour} and a ray, concerning a perch. The ray was not present for the signing.
Some Shulkin hum when they work. It is a thin, glassy sound. We never speak of it. If you hear one, pretend you do not, and they will hum a little louder.
A good lamplighter can tell the hour by the angle of the shadows. Not sunlit shadows; we have none. Rod shadows. It is an art. It is also mostly guesswork.
I once gave a speech in the Lid Hall for most of a lit hour. Two people stayed. One was asleep. I have never been happier.
There is a flat stone by the west bridge where the young ones carve their first words. 'Lamp' is the favourite. 'No' is the runner-up. Between them, they tell you everything.
I find it comforting that the void is so reliable. It is always exactly where I left it. Few things can say the same.
If you are ever lost in {village}, find a lamp and follow its cord. Every lamp is tied to the Lamp Tower. Eventually, so is everything else.
I never trust a sentence I have written in a hurry. I never trust one I have written slowly, either. That leaves a narrow strip of sentences. I live there.
On very quiet hours you can hear the island settle. A little pop. A long sigh. It is the sound of purpur remembering it used to be chorus.
I keep one shelf for books I plan to read. It has been full for ninety years. I have read none. I like having the plan.
The young ones ask me whether the Overworld is real. I say yes. They ask how I know. I say a friend told me. Then I feel strange for the rest of the lit hour.
I took a deep breath once before a speech. It made my lid rattle. I have not done it since. Calm, for a Shulkin, is a matter of staying very still.
They say you can tell a Shulkin's mood by how they carry their sleeves. Mine are carried in the manner of 'mildly interested, slightly anxious'. It is most days.
Mind where you step on the south bridge. The third plank is a different purpur from the rest. It was mended by someone in a rage. You can feel it.
If you want to make a Shulkin laugh, show them a very well-formatted list. It never fails. It is either that or a Driftray in a doorway.
{neighbour} says I take things too seriously. I told them I would record the observation. They said that was the problem.
Sometimes I listen to the young ones argue about who is tallest. They are all within a hand's height of each other. I do not correct them. Let them be tall a while.
There is one lamp in the Court nobody is allowed to trim. No one remembers why. We trim around it with great respect.
I have begun leaving the Reading Room door open when I think you might visit. The draught is dreadful. I am told it is very gracious.
The weaver says a good robe is forgotten by its wearer within an hour. I have worn mine sixty years and I still notice it. Either it is a poor robe or I am a poor wearer.
I keep the little bottles the Steads' cordial comes in. They ring when a draught passes. I have arranged them by pitch. {neighbour} calls it music. I call it filing.
We keep a spare lamp-hook by every door in the Spire, for lending. The hooks never come back, but the lending is considered very nearly the same thing as the returning.
My elder says I fidget in the Archive. It is true. My lid taps against my collar. They call it 'the small bell'. It keeps poor time, but it keeps me company.
6: When my lid first opened, the archivist wrote one word in my record: 'alert'. Underneath, smaller: 'if draughty'. My elders still call me Draughty.
I lost a friend to the void when I was young. A bridge, a missed step, no ray near enough. I write their name in the margin of every new volume.
Some nights I read the oldest records, from before the Long Watch. The hand is so calm. They didn't know what was coming. I envy them, and I don't.
Do you know what I'm afraid of? Not the Crowned. Not the void. An empty shelf. Something happening, and nobody writing it down.
{neighbour} and I quarrelled once, sixty years ago, over a comma. It still isn't settled. I think we both enjoy it too much.
When you're off on your travels, I check the bridge lamps more than I need to. I tell myself it's diligence.
Being Shulkin is mostly patience. We are very good at it. Sometimes I wonder if we are too good at it. We waited out a Dragon, instead of... well.
The Lid Hall seats three hundred. There are a dozen of us. We still meet there. Nobody suggests a smaller room. It would mean admitting something.
I used to think the record was the point. Lately I think the point is the person you read it to.
I once kept my lid shut for nine wakings over a broken promise. Childish. I would do it again. It was very restful.
You've seen more of the End in a year than I have in my life. I'm not jealous. I've written that down, so it's true.
There's a page in the Archive with your name on it. It's getting crowded. I've started writing smaller. I don't mind.
When I was young I wanted to be a wayfinder. Then I sat on a Driftray. It's fine. Not everyone needs to be up.
I was a poor student. The Nursery Keeper described me as 'attentive, in the manner of a Driftray'. I have never found out whether that was a compliment.
When I was young I wrote an epic poem about a lamp. It ran to nine hundred verses. It sits in the Vault, mislabelled as inventory. I have never corrected the label.
This is in no record. Once I walked to the Edge Lamp in the closed hours, to see whether I would dare to stay. I stayed until the bell. I shook the whole time. It was marvellous.
I have a habit I am not proud of: I read other people's volumes when they are out. Nothing scandalous. Mostly I look for spelling mistakes. I find a lot.
{neighbour} lent me a ray once, for one lit hour. I fell off it into the Roost netting and was carried home like a parcel. We do not discuss it.
There is a grief nobody names: the sound of a bridge you used to cross, when you have stopped crossing it. I hear it from the north span. It has gone quiet.
I think I would like a smaller job. Something small and exact. Tending a single lamp. Learning its every flicker.
I used to be sure of everything. Then I met someone whose certainties I could not file. I have been improving ever since.
Your voice carries a long way across the island. I hear you before I see you. It is a good sound. It sounds like someone telling the truth by accident.
I worry about being dull. A life of records, lamps and bells. Then you arrive with a story and I think: it is not so bad to be the one who keeps the place you return to.
My elder once told me I would never learn to forgive. I proved them right for forty years. Then I learned. It is an inconvenient skill; it makes you late for everything else.
I envy your fast days. You do a month's worth of living in one lit hour. I do an hour's worth of living in a month. Though I will say mine is thoroughly documented.
When I am nervous my lid chatters. It is very audible. The Nursery calls it 'the clatter'. They think I cannot hear them. I have excellent hearing.
Some nights I light my rod and read my own volume. It is like meeting a very reliable stranger. They have never lied to me, and never once surprised me. That is why I am so fond of you.
There was a time I wanted to be unremarkable. Utterly. A name in the margin of a thousand pages. Now I want to be remarkable to exactly one person. Do not ask which. Ha.
See this old crack along the lip of my shell? A fall from the Lamp Tower. I had climbed it on a dare. I won the dare. I also met the floor.
A friend is an odd thing for a record-keeper to own. I am trying to work out the filing. Under 'people'? Under 'luck'? It keeps falling out of every drawer.
I do not tell the others, but I am afraid of heights. A Shulkin in a Spire of towers, afraid of heights. I go up with my eyes shut, counting. I have counted to a very large number.
If I could have one wish, I would have a single lit hour in the old cities when they were whole. Not to rule them. Just to walk their halls, unobserved, and listen.
I was told once that I have the sort of face that makes strangers confess things. It is the lid. They think I am leaving room for them. I am usually thinking about supper.
Having a friend changes what you notice. I used to see an empty doorway. Now I see where someone might stand in it.
Two hundred years of careful handwriting, and the lines I am proudest of are the ones I wrote shaking. Odd, isn't it? The Archive disapproves.
I laughed so hard once that my lid stuck open for a full lit hour. The shellwright had to be fetched. We both agree it was worth it.
People think records are about the past. They are not. They are a letter to whoever opens the book next. I try to be kind to them.
I keep a few things on a shelf in my niche that mean nothing to anyone else: a bent rod, a chipped purpur tile, a scrap of void-cloth. I tell no one why. It is a short list of good days.
I am bad at silences. I fill them with weather, which we have not got. You are good at them. I would like to learn.
Sometimes I wonder what I would be if the Dragon had never come. Braver, perhaps. Or merely louder.
I tell the Nursery you are a very large, kind Driftray in disguise. It stops the arguments about whether you are a monster or a myth. The consensus is that you are, instead, a ray.
My habit of writing everything down began because I could not say it. Feelings are easier on the page. That is why I am so good at the page, and so bad at the doorway.
I try to be the sort of Shulkin who is quietly useful in a crisis. In truth I have never had a crisis. I have had inconvenient lit hours.
Once I tried to learn to dance. It is mostly standing in a line and pretending the floor is moving. The shellwright said I had talent. For the pretending.
I get a curious feeling when you have been gone a while: not quite loneliness. A sort of gap, with a lamp in it. I think that is what an absence looks like to a lamplighter.
If I could change one clause in the Bylaws, I would add: 'Visitors may be loved.' It is not there. We never needed it. We do now.
When we moved the Archive from the first shell to the second, we lost nine volumes and found three we had forgotten we owned. I call that a profit.
I find you restful, which is a strange thing to say of someone who fights, climbs and sets fire to things. It is the honesty. You do not hide your edges.
I practise my goodbyes. Not for you. In general. A Shulkin who can say goodbye properly can say hello with a clear conscience.
I miss the first lamp I was given. The little one that guttered, before they replaced it. I am told it was a fire risk. I am told many things.
I dreamed of a library where every book was blank, and nobody minded. We were all sitting in the dark, reading each other's faces. It was peaceful. I am still thinking about it.
They say a shell remembers the hand that last held it. My first teacher's shell rests in the Nursery. It feels warm under three fingers. I visit more than I admit.
When I am worried, I tidy. You would think I would have the neatest niche in the Spire. I have, in fact, the neatest niche in the Spire. It has been a worrying year.
The night you first came, I stayed awake writing. Page after page. Not the record. My own thoughts. I had so many. I threw nearly all of them out.
There is a lamp by the Archive stair that goes out whenever someone lies beneath it. So the story goes. I once told it I was fine. It flickered. I have avoided it since.
My favourite sentence in all the Archive is: 'And so it was found, upon enquiry, that nobody minded.' It closes a three-year dispute. I read it when I am cross.
You make me want to travel. Not far. A bridge or two. To see whether the lamps look different from the other side of the gap.
I do not enjoy being looked at, but I like being seen. It took me a century to learn the difference. You made it plain.
I am a coward in small things: a creaking plank, a loud hall, a sudden question. And braver than I look in the large ones. It is a peculiar way to be built.
A truth about record-keepers: we collect other people's endings. It is lovely when one of them comes back for an epilogue.
I have a theory that every Shulkin is a small, closed Archive, and every friend is the one who finally reads it aloud.
A gift, I have decided, is not about the item. It is about the thought of the person while choosing. I keep thinking of you, choosing.
My favourite kind of day is one in which nothing is recorded. Then I know it went well.
I am not as formal as I pretend. I practise the formality in a polished tile, and some days the rehearsal is a failure.
I once asked the Keeper how a lid knows when to open. They said it simply does, like a hand that wants to wave. I have been waving ever since, in a small way.
There is a bench by the Lamp Court I walk past. I always want to sit. I never do. I think I am waiting for someone to sit with.
I get a little nervous before you arrive, like before a recital. Then you walk in and the nerves go. I am not sure what the nerves were for.
The Archive taught me to write down what happened. You are teaching me to write down what it felt like. My pages are getting longer and a good deal less accurate.
9: When I close for the last time, {player}, I'd like you to be told. Not for the record. Just so someone who knew me open knows.
I've started a private volume. Not for the Archive. Things you've said that made me laugh. It's very thin, but it's mine.
We say a Shulkin is never alone while their shell is remembered. I never believed it until lately. I think it was about friends all along.
I read your page aloud in the Nursery. The young ones booed the Dragon and cheered you. Very unprofessional of me. I'd do it again.
If the Crowned ever come for {village}, the vault key is behind the third lamp. Don't write that down. Ha. Listen to me.
The lamp I'm named for was lit by a Chorrin, passing through with a cart of chorus. We don't allow that. Nobody has ever asked me. There. Now it's said.
I used to dream of the old cities as tombs. Since you came I dream of them with the doors open. I don't know what it means. I'm glad of it.
I used to fear the day the lamps go out. Now I fear the day you don't come back over the bridge. It's a smaller fear. It's worse.
I've decided something. When the record of {village} is sealed, your name goes on the first page, not the last. The others agreed. Mostly.
You've changed how I count time. I used to count it in lamps. Now I count it in your visits. That is a very un-Shulkin thing to admit.
Everyone who ever lived in {village} is in the Archive. Lately I wonder who'll remember me. Then you knock, and I stop wondering.
I'm old enough to be tired of most things. Not of this. Not of you turning up, dusty and impossible, with a story.
Sit with me a moment and don't say anything. The lamps are humming. That's all. I wanted someone to hear it with.
I have started to look forward to my own mistakes. They make such good stories to tell you.
I asked the weaver for a second mantle with a pocket sewn into it, because you once called pockets sensible. It is the most daring thing I have done. It holds very little. Today it holds a note.
Do you know what you have done? You have made me untidy. A margin, a doodle, a gap in the schedule. My elders have noticed. They think it is wonderful. I am unsure.
I used to think my lid opened for speech. It opens for you before I have anything to say. I have not told it to.
There is a drawer in my desk that I never open. It holds the first thing you said that made me laugh, written down in my worst handwriting. I do not open it because I know it by heart.
I have forgiven you for things you have not done yet. It saves time.
I have told the Nursery that your name is the first word the young ones should learn after 'lamp'. The Keeper said that was irregular. I said so was the Dragon's end.
Do you ever feel the Spire turn, ever so slightly, toward you? I know it does not. But when you arrive, everyone is facing the same direction.
If I could redraw the map of the End, I would put your name on the gaps. Not the islands. The gaps. That is where you live, I think.
I used to want a grand entry in the Archive. Now I would settle for being the first one you tell.
What would you put in your volume, if you had one? I have been compiling it for you in secret. It is not complete. I need your help with the middle.
I once asked the elders what it means to be home. They said, 'where the lamp is lit.' I think it may be, 'where the lamp is lit for you.'
I laughed in the Reading Room today. Out loud. All of it. Everyone stared. I regret nothing. It was your joke from last time, arriving late.
You should know the Archive has stopped asking me to file you. I think they have realised there is no drawer deep enough.
Whenever I am anxious I touch the shelf where your page is kept. It is an odd little ritual. The wood is warm there now. Or I have worn it down.
I have never been brave before the Court, the void or the dark. I was brave before you once, in a small way. It cost more than the rest put together.
Everything I have written about you is accurate. Everything I have not written is truer. It is a terrible arrangement for a record-keeper.
On slow lit hours I invent conversations with you. You are very wise in them. It is a pity the real you is only slightly wise and frequently covered in void-dust.
I always thought the last line of a volume was the hardest to write. It is not. It is the first line of the next, written before you know whether anything will happen.
I would walk onto the old bridges for you. The really old ones. The ones with the rails missing. I would go slowly, and with a great deal of muttering.
You have made the bells softer. Or I have learned to listen differently. They ring the hours, and I hear: there is time. There is still time.
I keep a second niche prepared, small and tidy, next to mine. I tell people it is for guests. They know.
If I am honest, I do not understand most of what you do. The climbing, the burning, the digging. I only understand that you do it and come back, and that is the part I am for.
I wrote you a rhyme. Rhyming is a Chorrin vice, but I tried. 'Lamp' and 'damp'. It is awful. It is yours.
I am told true friends can sit together and not feel the need to fill the quiet. I have made a note of it. It is the one note in my record that has no reference. It is simply true.
I told {neighbour} to treat you well, or answer to me. They laughed. I do not often make threats. I had been practising.
If I ever fail to open for you, check the hinge. It is only the hinge. The rest of me is on your side.
One day I counted the number of times you have made me laugh. I got to forty and stopped. It felt like cheating.
I think of all the people I have never met who will one day read about you. I hope they understand your jokes. I hope they understand the dust on your sleeves.
I wish you could taste the first chorus of the season, popped fresh from the kiln. It is the nearest thing to joy I can describe. The second nearest is you at the door.
You are the sort of person the Archive would invent, if it were allowed to invent. Thank the lamps it is not. You would have been tidier.
I once left a rod on your path so you would find your way in the closed hours. You did not notice. That was the point.
My elder asked me why I smile at the east bridge. I said it had good posture. They said it is a bridge. I said so I have heard.
The Spire is easier to love with someone to show it to. I was fond of it before. Now it has a reason.
I think of the lamps as old friends. I think of you as the first one who arrived without a lamp and lit the place anyway.
There are two kinds of silence I love: the Reading Room's, and the one beside you. I am not sure which I would choose. The Reading Room has fewer opinions.
I used to leave my desk in perfect order each night. Now I leave a page open, just in case you turn up with something to add.
Some days I wonder if I am too happy to be good at my work. Then I check the record. It is very good. Better than ever. So, no.
You have taught me that a Shulkin can be wrong and live. I have been wrong forty times this season. I am thriving.
I would give you a lamp-name if I could. 'Of the Lamp Left Lit.' Do not groan. It is all I could think of.
I noticed today that I have stopped bracing when the door opens. That is you. That is all you.
I wanted to say something wise. I have nothing. So here it is, plain: I am glad of you. Please carry on.
You are the only person I have ever wanted to tell about a bad day, and a good one, and a day that was neither. It is wonderful and terrible.
If you are ever lonely out there, the deep, wide kind of lonely, think of me counting lamps and arriving at your name. It is how I fall asleep now.
I was not made for this. For fondness, I mean. It leaks. It gets into the margins. It has got into my handwriting, and now the letters lean toward the door.
Everything the Spire taught me was about holding on to things. You are teaching me to put them down and trust they will still be there.
I would like to hear you laugh in the Lid Hall, just once. Three hundred seats, and the echo would have to work for the first time in a century.
I do not say it often, but when the lamps dim in the closed hours I think of you out there, still walking, still unfinished, and I hope the dark is kind to you.
Do you know the best part of the day? The moment just before you speak, when your face decides what to say. I have never once guessed right. I love that.
I have given up pretending that I am only polite to you. You can see through me. It is a surprisingly comfortable sort of transparency.
I used to wonder whether a friend would be a distraction. It turns out a friend is the thing I was being distracted from.
I have begun humming while I write. I did not mean to. It has no tune. {neighbour} says it sounds like contentment. I told them to mind their own ledger.
In the first years of my volume I wrote for the reader after me. Now I write for the reader beside me. The handwriting has improved. Isn't that curious?
I was afraid I would spend my life telling the truth to shelves. Now I tell it to you, and it comes back with a laugh. Thank you for being a better echo than the Lid Hall.
If this is what the old Shulkin meant by a lamp burning for someone, I understand the whole tradition now. Pass it on. No, write it down. Pass it on, then write it down.

0: The Dragon circled the old cities for longer than the Archive has shelves. And you silenced it. We are still learning to say that sentence calmly.
For centuries we hooded our lamps on the side facing the centre, so the Dragon would not see them. Some hoods are still on. Habit is a stubborn shell.
When it fell, every lamp in the Spire flickered at once. The lamplighters swear they had nothing to do with it.
We did not fight it. We waited. Shulkin are very good at waiting. The Dragon was very good at not leaving. It was a long contest.
The Archive refuses the Dragon a name. A name is a page, and we would not give it one. We call it 'the Circle', which is only what it did.
Its roar was never heard so much as worn. Every shell in the Spire rang, low, for as long as it flew. The old ones say you stopped noticing. The old ones are polite liars.
Its breath left violet smears on the south towers. The shellwrights have scrubbed for centuries. I suspect the stains will outlast the scrubbers.
The first night after the silence we lifted one hood, the one facing the centre. For the first time in an age our light crossed the gap. Nobody said a word.
We kept a bell for the Dragon: three rings if it was seen near the Spire. It has rung once since the silence. A Driftray sat on the rope. We were very polite about it.
Before the Dragon was loosed, the centre was merely 'the Centre'. During, it was 'where it circles'. We have not yet agreed what to call it now.
From our bridges we watched ten points of light go dark on the far island, one after another. I counted aloud. I am told I was loud.
Children here play 'Hood the Lamp': one circles with arms spread, the rest shut their lids and hide. Lately they let the Dragon lose. The Keeper is considering the implications.
There is a rule in the Lamp Court against whistling. A whistle sounds like a wing. The rule stands, though I doubt any of us still remembers how to whistle.
It never landed on our island, you understand. It kept to the old cities and the centre. We hooded our lamps against its eye, not its wings. Fear is also a kind of architecture.
The worst of a long siege is not the fear. It is the habits it leaves. We still lower our voices when the lamps dim. We did it long after anything was listening.
My account of the silence is one line. The Archive's runs to nine pages. People prefer mine, which tells you something about the Archive.
Some in {village} wish to thank you with a lamp in your name. The committee has met nine times. They have agreed on the lamp and are now fighting about the hook.
A shell that survives a Dragon is called 'rare'. A shell that outlasts it is called 'old'. Most of us here are both, and neither is boasting.
Do not mistake our calm for forgetting. We are calm the way a closed lid is calm. There is a great deal going on behind it.
On the silence-day we all stop at the hour it fell and listen to nothing for as long as the bell hangs in the air. The young find it dull. The elders call it the best part of the year.
A column of light rose from the centre when it fell. We saw it from every bridge. The Archive notes it as 'pale, tall, without warmth'. I have a more personal note, and am asked to stop adding to it.
Statues of the Dragon were forbidden here. Not from reverence: so it would not be flattered. Now the young carve it from chorus stalks and give it small hats. The Archive has stopped objecting.
Some say the Dragon sang: a high, thin note before each circle, too high for most to hear. I was one of the few who did. I still hear it sometimes in the hum of the end rods.
3: Was it frightened, at the end? Forgive me. The Archive wants to know. So do I, which is less professional.
My elder's elder saw the Dragon loosed. They wrote one line about it, then nothing for three years. The blank pages are the worst part of the Archive.
The Crowned loosed it. Remember that, whatever they tell you. The Dragon was only the arrow. The Court drew the bow.
I'm told some of you bring it back, to fight it again. Please don't. We have only just put the hoods away.
The Dragon came before the Long Watch, but it was the Long Watch that wore us down. A Dragon one can fear. A circle one can only endure.
Two Spires in my lamp's line went silent in its breath. The towers stand, and so do the shells that were inside. We still tend them.
People think the Dragon was our worst enemy. The Archive thinks the worst was the quiet between circles, when we could not tell whether it was gone or merely thinking.
I once read the first account of its loosing. The writer used the word 'sudden' four times on one page. An archivist who loses their adjectives is an archivist in danger.
When it flew, we put cloth over the young in the Nursery and sang the counting-song so they would not hear the roar. It is the only song most of us know. We are trying to learn another.
Did you see its eye? Our only picture is a scratch on a wall in an old city. It looks like a wheel. I hope there was more to it than that.
Our lamps did one thing the Dragon disliked: they were small. It could not choose among them. A great fire it would have found. Four hundred small ones it could not count.
I keep a rod at my window facing the centre. It has stayed bare since the silence. I told no one it was for you. I said it was for the view.
After the silence the Chorrin sent a crate of chorus and a message, hummed by a breathless blinker: 'Celebrate, you fusspots.' It is on the Lid Hall wall. We did celebrate. Quietly. By the bell.
There is a debate whether the Dragon was a beast or an instrument. I vote beast. An instrument does not keep circling when no one is giving orders.
Wayfinders learned the void currents by watching which way the Dragon swept. A terrible teacher. Excellent charts.
I would like to see where it fell. Not to look at it. To stand there and confirm that the silence is real.
My shell has a chip near the hinge from the day the roar shook the Nursery. I am vain about it. It is the only interesting thing about me.
They say the sky above the centre is different now. Emptier. We have never had much of a sky, yet it is odd to miss what was in it.
I used to count in circles. 'Three circles ago.' 'Before the fifth.' I keep catching myself. The Dragon outlived its own measure.
They say it left an egg. The Archive has a question about that and has decided the question can wait until after dinner. For a century. It is an old and reliable tactic.
You collect its breath in bottles? And carry them about? I will not ask what for. I would only like them kept far from the Nursery.
Whenever a bell rings twice in a hurry, the oldest of us still flinch. We make a joke of it. It is not funny. It is the only joke we have.

The Chorrin hid in their groves. We hid under cloth. The Court sat in its Citadels. If you ever write the Long Watch, make the Dragon the smallest part. The largest was what people did in their rooms.
6: I used to dream the Dragon landed on our Lamp Tower and simply looked at me. I haven't had that dream since you came. I wanted you to know.
You fought it with the crystals burning and the Unlidded watching. Alone. I couldn't have. I've thought about that a great deal.
The Archive calls you 'the one who silenced the Dragon'. I call you {player}. I'm told that's irregular. Let them tell me.
A confession, for the record. During the Long Watch I once wished the Dragon would simply take us and end the waiting. I was young, bored and very frightened. I have told no one.
When you left for the centre I sat on the east bridge for three bells. I did not light anything. I felt that being seen to wait would be unlucky. Waiting is a superstition too.
When the first rumour came that it was dead, I felt relief. Then shame, because I had done nothing. Then relief again, because shame is a luxury of the safe.
The Dragon took my elder's voice before it took anything else. After the second circle they never spoke above a whisper. I speak up now, on their behalf.
Do you know what I do when I am frightened? I recite the Bylaws of the Lamp Court. Clause nine. It has never once helped. I have never once stopped.
I wonder what the Dragon wanted. Not the Court. The Dragon. Whether anything circles for centuries without a wish of its own. You looked it in the eye. You would know.
There was a cold night when I thought the roar was inside my own chest. It was a Driftray beneath the bridge. I have never been so embarrassed, or so grateful.
You grip a bridge rail like someone who has already decided to be brave. I have been practising the grip on the east bridge. The Driftrays beneath it are unimpressed.
I talk to my elder's lamp-hook, hung beside my door, about the Dragon. I tell them it is over. Hooks don't answer. I feel better regardless.
The nights I dread now are the quiet ones. In the Long Watch a quiet night meant it was elsewhere. Now it means nothing, and nothing frightens me more than I would like.
I wrote a very bad poem about the silence. It rhymes 'wing' with 'ring' and 'everything'. I have burnt it. I mean that literally. A lamp was to hand.
The young ones asked whether you were afraid. I said no, for their sake. You were afraid, weren't you? Good. I would trust you less otherwise.
I assumed the end of the Dragon would feel like a victory. It feels like a held breath finally let go. That is different, and better, and takes longer to get used to.
I dream of the Long Watch sometimes: the roar, the hoods, the cloth over the young. I wake and the Spire is quiet. Then I am grateful. I have never said so aloud. I'm saying it now.
If it ever seems to follow you, come to the Lamp Tower. I will put a rod in every window that faces the centre. It is what we do for a friend in the dark.
In the last year, before you came, it stopped circling for three days. The Archive wrote 'rest'. I wrote 'dread'. My elder wrote nothing. Nobody slept.

Writing dates is hard now. We used to write 'before the fourth circle'. The Archive is adopting a new reckoning. I voted for 'since the silence'. We lost to 'the Year of the Hook'. It is a long story.
I am glad you did not do it for our sake. We would owe you, and we have so little. As it is you are only a friend with a deed behind you, and friends may be thanked in small coin.

Someone here tried to feed the Dragon once, setting popped chorus on the bridge-head each hour. It was never taken. They kept on for sixty years. We called them mad. I think they alone practised hope.
9: Sometimes I'm almost sorry for it. Bound to the Court, circling an empty city for an age. Is that strange? You're the only one I'd say it to.
When the Dragon died, we lost the thing we were waiting out. Some of us don't know what to wait for now. I wait for your visits.
If it ever came back, I'd want to be standing next to you. Not behind. Next to. Write that down for me; I'm too frightened to.
One night in the Long Watch a lamplighter left a hood off, facing the centre, on purpose. The Dragon hung outside for an hour, then left. The record is filed under 'weather'. Nobody reads Weather.
I think the lamplighter did it out of pity. A thing circling alone for an age with no one looking at it. We hooded our lights so it would not see us. Imagine how that felt, if it felt.
I gave the Dragon a name once, in a very small voice, when I was young. I won't say it. One does not repeat the name of a thing one has outlived. But I wanted you to know I did.
The night of the silence I walked onto the bridge and opened my lid wide to the whole dark and shouted. I have no idea what. A neighbour recorded it. I have paid them not to read it.
If the Dragon has a ghost, it is not in the old cities. It is in us: the hooded habit, the lowered voice. You can't cut that with a blade, {player}. But you can sit with it. You do. You sit with me.
I am not brave. The Archive says 'patient', which is brave's cousin who stays indoors. But I have decided that if it ever came back I would open my lid and say your name to it. Only that.
My elder's last words were about the Dragon: 'Don't let them forget to be afraid.' I think it is the wrong lesson. One can remember and still sleep. You are the proof.
The Spire keeps a feast on the silence-day now, and every year someone asks who to thank. I say 'a visitor'. It is not a lie. It is an unfinished sentence.
I used to think the Dragon was the end of the story: the thing we waited out. Now I think it was only a page. The book is yours and mine, and mostly blank. Come and help me fill it.
I kept one hood, out of all the hundreds. It hangs by my bed, dull purpur, slightly bent. I took it down myself, on the first night. It is yours when I close. Hang it facing the centre.
When I think of the roar I think of you walking toward it. It is the only way the memory is bearable: with you in the middle of it, small, going the right way.
Whenever I say I am not afraid of it returning, I am lying, and you have never once corrected me. Thank you for leaving that lie in the margin.
Some mornings I still check the sky. And some mornings, I admit, it is you I am looking for in it.
If I write the Long Watch as one book, I will end it not on the silence but on the first lit hour you walked up the east bridge. Dragons end. Visitors begin things.
Here is the truest thing I know about the Dragon: it did not make me braver. You did. Fear teaches nothing. A friend teaches nearly everything. Sit. I will light the good rod.
I used to be ashamed that we only waited, lit our lamps and hid under cloth. You made me see that waiting is also a way to stand. Not your way. Ours. It kept the young alive.
When I close, leave the Dragon out of my record. Let it say: 'Lived in the time of the Dragon, died in the time of the silence.' And a line beneath: 'Was visited.'

0: Work? I am between offices. The Lid Hall assures me this is an honour. I assure the Lid Hall that it is not.
I keep the Spire's general record. That is, I notice things. It is a calling with no robe and very poor pay.
I help where I'm needed. Mostly I'm needed to hold the other end of things.
The shellwrights have promised me an apprenticeship. They promised it in a very slow voice.
3: I tally the chorus deliveries from the Chorrin. Never late, never on time. They come when the fruit is ready, and the fruit won't be hurried.
Unofficially, I tell the lamplighter which rods flicker. Officially, I'm a nuisance.
I polish the Eye in the Lamp Court tiles. Every tile, every lit hour. It doesn't need it. Someone ought to do it anyway.
6: Honestly, {player}? I've never found the work that fits. Everyone else's lamp burns a certain colour. Mine just burns.
I sat a year at the archivist's elbow and a year at the weaver's loom. I was adequate at both. 'Adequate' is in my record twice.
Perhaps my work is to remember the people who do the work. Someone has to keep the keepers.
9: I think my work now is being your friend in {village}. Unpaid, unrecorded, and the best office I've held.
If you ask for nothing, they forget to give you a post, and you get to talk to visitors. That's my whole secret.
When you leave, I go to the Roost and watch the gaps until you're past them. If that's a job, I'm very good at it.

0: This island has held {village} since the Long Watch began. The bridges came later. The first generation simply did not visit each other.
Every building here is shaped like a shell: a body, a glowing gap, a lid. We build what we are. It saves on explanations.
The Lamp Tower stands tallest because light carries furthest from high up, and the dark is where the Unlidded walk in.
A Lid Hall, an Archive, a Nursery and a great many stairs. Mind the bridges. The rails are recent and nobody fully trusts them.
You'll want to meet {neighbour}. Everyone does, eventually. It's quicker than trying to avoid them.
The Gapbook is kept at the east bridge-head. Its last guest signed before the Long Watch, and the ink has gone the colour of weak tea. Do add yours.
We glide, but we build stairs. Stairs are for ceremony, and for remembering that we once had to climb. The Chorrin find them hilarious. They climb them twice.
The bell rings once for the lit hours and twice for the closed. Between the two comes the Quiet Hour, when nobody speaks and everybody reads. Please do not greet anyone in it.
Our windows are magenta glass, so every lamp is tinted and the whole Spire glows the colour of a held breath. Visitors call it beautiful. We call it efficient.
On the bridges, whoever carries more yields. It has caused eleven polite deadlocks, two of them in the same week.
A lid cannot lift for speech while the mouth is full. Dinner in the Lid Hall is therefore a long, elegant taking of turns.
We name our stairs, particularly the ones that creak. 'Complaint'. 'Second Thoughts'. 'The Archivist's Knee'. You will be told which is which only after you have trodden on them.
The Loft above the Lid Hall is where void-cloth is woven. It is the warmest room in {village} and the only one where humming is permitted. The weavers say it helps the threads.
Almost no door in {village} is locked. Doors are closed, which is a different thing. The difference is several hundred years of manners.
A Driftray has right of way on every bridge by long custom. Several of us have waited an hour at a crossing for a ray to finish a thought.
We count a year by the trimming of the Great Rod, the biggest lamp in the Lamp Tower. It is trimmed once, at the Yearturn. The rest of the time it is merely very bright.
The shortest street in {village} is called Long Street. The Archive keeps a note on the matter. The note is longer than the street.
Each of us has a place reserved on the Niche Wall in the Lid Hall, with a lamp beside it, for after we close. Mine is empty so far. I try not to look in as I pass. One does not wish to seem eager.
Letters travel by ray. A Driftray takes six bells to the next Spire and always arrives. It does not always arrive at the right window.
Guests are traditionally lent a paper lid for the Hall. Nobody remembers what it is for. The tradition is older than the reason.
At the Yearturn every Spire mends one thing: a rail, a stair, a lamp-hook. The record shows we mend the same rail every year. It is a favourite. It is extremely well mended.
The Hall's long table is laid with one place empty at every meal, for the closed. Nobody sits there. Nobody has ever suggested we stop.
Every dwelling in {village} has a lamp-hook by the door and a second, lower hook beside it, for the young. Nobody knows which was added first. The Archive calls it 'a family argument'.

Nothing is thrown away in {village}. Broken rods become toys. Cracked glass becomes a Nursery window. Worn cloth becomes bandage, then lining, then a lid-wipe. We call it thrift. It is really manners.
3: {neighbour} has borrowed my second-best lamp hook for eleven years. The Archive holds the receipt. I bring it up at every festival.
We are small here, but very well documented. You could find out what anyone ate on any lit hour of the last century. Nobody ever wants to.
The Nursery is the loudest place in {village}. Young lids pop open at everything. It sounds like a kiln full of chorus.
We voted on the bridge rails. It took a decade. Meanwhile three people fell. Two were caught by Driftrays. The rails won.
Every Yearturn we swap rods with the next Spire: ours go over, theirs come back. Nobody knows why. The first swap is lost to the record. The second was a grudge. The third is simply tradition.
We keep a Shelf of Things Left on Bridges: one pointed boot, a sealed letter to no one, a single glove mended many times. Nobody has claimed the glove in a century. We keep mending it.
We schedule the Archive readings for the same hours as the Nursery games, so the young ones have something to drown out. The readers have developed excellent projection.
There is a lamp on the third bridge that burns green. It was a flaw in the rod. The lamplighters have decided it is 'character'.
The Lid Hall seats three hundred and has been dusted by the same two pairs of hands for sixty years. I am told they have never met. They leave notes. It is the longest friendship in {village}.
At each naming the Keeper traces the new lid on a leaf of paper and files it. Mine has gone brown, and it is a very bad tracing, because I wriggled. I adore it.
The young are taught to close their lids at a stranger's step and open them when the step says 'good lamp'. It still works on {neighbour}.
Once a year the Archive reads the Lamp Roll aloud: every lamp lit in the Spire since the Long Watch, with its keeper's name. It takes nine bells. The Nursery is excused. The Nursery attends.
A lamp-hook is the only gift we truly give. It is carved with the lamp of the one who receives it. Mine, from my elder, is plain and worn, and I would not trade it for the vault.
When a ray lands on the top of the Lamp Tower, the whole Spire sways, very slightly. The lamplighters call it 'the nod'. We pretend not to notice. It is good for everyone's spirits.
The shellwrights cut a Spire so lamplight falls on a face exactly as a lid lifts. It is why none of us ever takes the long way home. We like the effect.
One niche in the east wall of the Lid Hall is empty on purpose, with a lamp lit before it. It is for 'whoever comes next'. Nobody says who. I have my private opinion.
{neighbour} and I share a bridge, a bell and a grievance. Two of the three are in the record.
On the landing halfway up the Lamp Tower sits a stool, the Stool of Honest Opinion. Anyone who climbs that far is asked what they think of the climb. The entries are not flattering.
We keep a list of the kinds of silence in {village}: the Quiet Hour, the silence before a naming, the silence after one of {neighbour}'s jokes. The list stands at fourteen and is disputed.
The young may not use the highest bridge until their lids have darkened. The Keeper says the height is not the danger. The danger is the view, and the ideas it gives them.
We keep a festival called Lid Day, when everyone opens fully at once for the length of a bell. No speaking, no writing. It is the only time {village} is wholly honest. It is frightfully embarrassing.
The Archive and the Nursery share a wall. For a century the archivists complained of the noise. For another they have complained of the silence when the young are at lessons. We are never satisfied.
The smallest room in the Spire is the Room of Reasonable Doubt, where the Archive settles disputes. It seats two. The same two have sat in it for forty years. They no longer remember the argument.
6: {neighbour} pretends not to like you. They asked me three questions about you since the last bell. That's three more than they ask about anyone.
I know every creak in {village}. Lately there's a new one: yours, coming over the east bridge. I listen for it.
I've seen three lamplighters retire here. Each one said the rods were dimmer than in their day. Each one was right, slightly.
When someone is overdue, we turn a lamp to face the way they went. It does nothing. We do it anyway. There is one on the east side that is turned toward you more often than I will admit.
I know this Spire's sounds as I know my own hinge: the stair that sighs, the rod that ticks, the bridge that says one small word when a ray passes. When you are away, it sounds like it is listening.
There is a corner of the Reading Room, by the lowest lamp, where I sit after bad news. The shell beside mine has sat there longer. I do not know their name. We have never spoken. It helps.
I once spent a year working out what the Spire lacked. A place to sit outdoors. I built a bench on the north bridge. It is the most-used building in {village}. Nobody knows it was me.
My place on the Niche Wall is third from the left. I chose it when young and certain. Now I visit it as one visits a distant relation. I would prefer it nearer the Nursery. Don't write that down.
In the Long Watch the Spire kept a rule that no one should be alone at the closing hour. It was never repealed. It is why I sit with {neighbour} at the bell even when we are not speaking.
I fear {village} may become a place of closed shells and a few open ones. We are shrinking, you know. There are fewer namings every century. The Nursery is loud, but it is small.
I believe the Spire likes visitors. I have seen the lamps along the east bridge brighten when someone crosses. The lamplighter denies it. They also deny talking to the rods.
In my youth I meant to leave and found a Spire of my own. I got as far as the last bridge. I looked back at the lamps and turned round. I have never regretted it. I have never forgotten it either.
If you want to know what {village} thinks of you, ask the Nursery. They have given you a nickname. I am not permitted to tell you. It is quite flattering, and involves a Dragon.
It is our custom to leave a rod lit in the window for a returning friend. Mine has been lit since you were last here. I am told that is not what the rods are for. I have decided it is.
The Archive holds a map of the islands from before the bridges, when each was a separate tower that rarely spoke to the others. We are one village that remembers having been many.
I watched this village grow quieter and quieter and could not say when it began. Then you came, and it grew quiet in a different way. I am still learning the difference.
There is a loose tile in the Lamp Court I step over each time. Fifty years. It is my private landmark. If it is ever mended I shall walk the same arc round it, and feel foolish, and fond.
The trouble with a small village is that one cannot quarrel and walk away. One quarrels and then sits down to dinner. It is the best and worst thing about us.
When a lamp goes out we do not relight it at once. We sit with it for a bell and ask what it was trying to tell us. Usually it was old. Sometimes it was lonely. We are not good at telling which.
There is a window in the Archive that looks over all of {village}. At each turn of the hour I count the lit windows. The number never changes. I count anyway. It is how I know we are still here.
I take the long way to my work every day, past the Nursery windows, so I can hear the young. It adds a quarter-bell. I tell no one it is the best part of my walk.
The Spire has a smell: warm purpur, end-rod dust, a little cloth. Coming home from the Crossing it is the first thing I notice. The second is how I missed it. The third is usually you, on the bridge.
9: If {village} ever has to move, I've listed what to carry. The Archive, the young ones, the lamps. You're on it. Don't argue; it's in ink.
When I'm gone, {neighbour} will keep my shelf. I've asked them to keep a page free for you. They grumbled. That's a yes.
The whole of {village} has decided you're one of us, as much as anyone without a lid can be. There was no vote. Everyone simply started setting a place.
The first Archivist buried a lamp beneath the Lid Hall floor, lit and sealed. They say it burns yet. I have never dared check. I choose to believe it: a small light we all stand on.
There is a door in the vault with no key. The oldest rumour in {village} says it opens onto the first Nursery, from before the Long Watch. Every naming day I lay my palm against it. It is warm.
I am leaving you something in my will. The Archive has no such form; I had to invent one. It is a single page. It names you, my lamp-hook, and the right to sit in my chair when you visit. Please do.
Sometimes I walk the whole of {village} at the hour when everyone is closed, and say good lamp to each door. Nobody hears. I am not a sentimental person. I am a person with a great many doors.
I never told you: the east bridge was relit for you. Not for a festival, not for anyone. I asked the lamplighter, and they did not ask why. That is how I know they are fond of you too.
The only unanimous vote since the Long Watch was whether your name could be read at the Lamp Roll, among the lamps. Nobody remembered ever agreeing on anything. It was most surprising.
At the Yearturn I mean to ask the Keeper to light a lamp for you in the Nursery. Not a naming lamp: a welcome. The young ones will ask who it is for. I shall say, 'A relative.' It is not untrue.
I once thought {village} was the only place I could breathe. Then you described an Overworld where people breathe in every direction. I am still jealous. And I am still here. One can be both.
If I ever had to choose between the Archive and the Nursery in a fire, I would choose the Nursery. I have told the Archive. It took it hard. It is paper; it will recover.
There is a spare lamp-hook beside my door. I have never said who it is for. It is yours. Hang what you like on it. A cloak. A sword. A dragon-egg, if you must.
We have a custom I have never explained. When a visitor leaves, everyone looks at the bridge until they are out of sight. Everyone. Even the busy. I think it is the kindest thing we do.
I used to believe the best thing about home was how little it changed. Now I think the best thing is that someone could arrive and change it. You did. Please don't stop.
Whatever else is written of this Spire, I want it known that for a while a great many ordinary shells were very happy. I keep a page for it. Your name is in its margin, which has the most ink.
Do you know why we keep so many lamps lit? The old reason was the Unlidded. The true one, I think, is that we fear a dark in which nobody knows we are here. You always know we are here. Thank you.
When I picture {village} in a hundred years I put a visitor on the east bridge, dusty, loud, with a sack of improbable gifts. Someone goes out to meet them. I hope it is someone like me.
I wrote a letter to be read at my closing. It is mostly about {village}. Not the Archive or the lamps: the small things. The east bridge, the green lamp, you. I want the Hall full for it.
If {village} ever has to be rebuilt, I would have it a little lower. I think we built so high out of fear. I would like us to be a village you could step into from the ground.
When I was small my elder showed me {village} from the top of the Lamp Tower and said, 'This is what we are for.' I thought they meant the lamps. They meant: a place a person can come back to.
I am fonder of {village} than I have admitted, and of you than I will. If I were asked where to close, I would say the east bridge, where I can hear you coming.

0: The Chorrin? Our oldest partners. Every wall here is purpur, purpur is popped chorus, and the chorus was theirs. We built our cities out of their harvests.
They hum instead of speaking. You get used to it. After a century you start humming back by accident, which they find hilarious.
We call it the Old Accord: we built, they grew. Then the Dragon came, and the Accord became a correspondence.
They blink away when startled. Vanish, and turn up a few steps over. We slam our lids. Every people has its dignity.
A Chorrin cook once offered me a bowl. I said I do not eat in public. They said it was not public, it was a kitchen. I have thought about this for forty years.
A Chorrin crown flowers with its owner's mood. One cannot lie to a Chorrin, and one cannot be lied to by one. We find it restful and slightly indecent.
Their villages are called Steads, and they are half sunk into the ground. We build up. They build down. Between us a whole island is accounted for.
At a Crossing the market is shared: a spire quarter and a stead quarter round one square. The square is where we are at once most polite and most suspicious.
The Chorrin pay in chorus and kiln-baked goods. We pay in cloth, lamps and receipts. They say the receipts are worth nothing. They keep every one.
They wear a buckle of shell on their belts. They swear it is shed shell, given freely. I have chosen to believe them, and not to look closely at the buckle.
They call the Unlidded 'the Tall Quiet'. It is kinder than our name for them. I have never managed to be as kind.
A Chorrin once blinked into the Reading Room mid-sneeze. The Archive survived. The sneeze went into the record as an act of nature.
Chorrin count time in 'blooms' and distance in 'hums'. The conversion, I am told, depends on how the hum is feeling. We no longer trade by distance.
We envy the Chorrin nothing, except the groves, the songs, and the way they laugh. I realise that is three things. Do not hold me to the first sentence.
They keep Grovebacks, those six-legged grazers with gardens on their backs. We keep Driftrays. The Chorrin say a ray is a beast that has given up. We say a Groveback is a hill with opinions.
A Chorrin crown, left untended, grows into the roof. Several Stead roofs have been cut for this reason. It is considered a compliment to the household.
In my youth I tried to learn the hum. I produced a sound they described as 'a shell dropped on stone'. They were being kind. It was a shell dropped on stone.
The Chorrin have no word for 'archive'. They say 'the place where the Shulkin keep what we sang'. It is longer, but it is correct.
Be careful with their hospitality. It is sincere, and it is endless, and it involves a great deal of chorus. One leaves a Stead heavier and happier and a little bit lost.
The Chorrin consider our silence a kind of speech. They are right. We consider their humming a kind of silence. We are also right. It took a century to see that it is the same thing.
A Chorrin once told me the Archive looked sad. I looked again, and had a window cut. The records are better lit. They are also, I admit, a little more cheerful.
The Chorrin call us 'the Polite'. It is not a compliment, nor wholly an insult. We call them 'the Warm', and make no such distinction. We are not sure which of us has the better of it.
At a Crossing the Chorrin bring their own seats to a meeting and the Shulkin bring their own scribes. Neither side has ever been caught without. It is the basis of all diplomacy.
3: Chorrin are warm and blunt and loud. Shulkin are cool and careful and quiet. Put us in a room and it's either a feast or a treaty dispute.
I like them. Quietly. Say it aloud and they hug you, and they're made of stone, and I'm made of shell. A bad combination.
They never write anything down. They remember in songs. I've tried to record the songs. They change them on purpose, I'm sure of it.
A Chorrin once asked what I keep in my shell. I said 'myself'. They laughed for an hour. I still don't know what was funny.
At Stead feasts everyone brings the dish they are worst at. It is custom: shared failure, shared food. I attended once. The soup was tragic. I recorded it as a triumph.
A Chorrin gave me a cutting of chorus for my window. It has grown three flowers in as many years and is the only thing in my room that does not need me. I have never been so touched.
A Chorrin cannot keep a secret; the crown blooms a different colour when they try. It makes them trusting company. You know exactly what they are hiding, and so do they.
At Crossing markets the Chorrin haggle by humming, the pitch rising with the price. The Shulkin bargain in writing. Visitors say the Crossing is a concert or a court, depending on the hour.
A Hum Circle is a ring of standing stones where everyone sits and hums a village into agreement. We have a Lamp Court. Theirs is faster. I decline to say which I prefer.
They think our lamps lovely and impractical. We think their groves lovely and impractical. The Old Accord rests on gentle misunderstandings of this sort.
I asked a Chorrin how they remember so much without writing. They said, 'We don't. We remember the shape of it and sing the rest.' I have tried both ever since. I am worse at the singing.
At the Crossings, the Nurseries and the sprout-groves swap a few young for a week each year. They arrive loud and leave louder. The Keeper says the walls take three days to recover.
Between Chorrin the greeting is to touch crowns. We lift our lids instead. Between Chorrin and Shulkin it is a ceremony of two people showing each other their best feature.
A Chorrin hums at the dead. We write them. I used to think the difference was cultural. Now I suspect the Chorrin simply noticed that the dead cannot read.
They have a saying: 'Never trust a person who cannot be startled.' The Shulkin hear it as an insult. I hear it as a description of the Archive.
The Chorrin brew a drink of fermented chorus that makes a crown blush. I took one sip. My lid would not lift for an hour. The brewer said it was the nicest I had ever looked.
In the Steads the doors are round. A round door cannot be slammed; it only closes, with a kind of sigh. I envy this, being a person who can only slam.
Their kilns pop the fruit into purpur with a crack I felt in my shell the first time. Now it is the sound I sleep to on a Crossing night. I did not choose that.
Chorrin sprouts are hugged by everyone, constantly. Our young are admired from a respectful distance. I cannot say which is better for them. The sprouts seem happier. Ours seem tidier.
The Shulkin and the Chorrin once tried to share a calendar. We count by lamps. They count by blooms. The compromise was 'sometime'. It has served for four hundred years.
Chorrin sprouts at the Crossing stare at our lids as if they might do a trick. We lift them slightly. The sprouts shriek with delight. It is the best audience I have ever had.
The first Chorrin I ever met took my hand and led me across a bridge. I was a hundred and twelve. I had crossed that bridge alone a thousand times. I was too moved to say so.
Chorrin etiquette says a gift is given in secret and received in public. Ours says the reverse. A gift passing from Spire to Stead must be hidden twice and revealed twice. It takes all afternoon.
6: We're equals now. Partners. The record says so. But it also remembers that, in the old cities, they lived on the lower floors. Some of them remember too.
When the Dragon came, the Chorrin hid our young in their groves. The Archive has the names. I read them every year. They don't know we do that.
I'm wary of them, a little. They're wary of us. That's honest, at least. The Crowned are never wary; they're certain. I'll take honest.
In my life I have had three messages from a Chorrin, each three notes long. I answered each with a volume. They have never complained. I think they use the volumes to prop doors.
A Chorrin once fell asleep at my Archive desk, the crown wound round my inkwell. I wrote a whole page round them and left the page where it lay. It is the best page I own.
I saw a Chorrin weep at a Crossing market, the crown dropping every petal at once. The whole stall went silent. I held their hand. I did not know I could.
What I envy in them is that they may be afraid in public. We write our fear down and shelve it. They let the crown droop and everyone sits beside them. It seems a better system.
A Chorrin at the Crossing blooms pale blue when I come near. I have never seen the colour on anyone else. They deny it is for me. It is for me.
Some evenings I sit at the edge of the Hum Circle in the Crossing. They never ask me to join. They hum a little softer, so I can hear the shape. It is the best manners I know.
They say we are the cold ones. I say they are the loud ones. Both are true. Each of us is secretly the other, on a good day.
We keep records of everything. The Chorrin keep everything else. If the Archive burned, I would ask a Chorrin what we were. If their groves burned, they would ask me. That is the whole Accord.
I taught a Chorrin to read their own name. They taught me to sit still without writing. Neither of us is any good yet.
At a Crossing feast a Chorrin put a chorus flower in my collar without asking. It stayed there a month. Nobody remarked on it. The next month I put one in theirs. We have not discussed it.
They find it funny that we shut our lids when embarrassed. They do not understand that for us it is a solemn act. They also do not understand that this is why it is funny.
The Chorrin say they fear nothing but the void. I believe them. I also believe that is half the reason they sing: to fill it. I have never heard such brave noise.
If a Chorrin friend fell from a bridge while I watched, I would go after them. I know it is foolish. I have written 'foolish' beside it and signed.
We call it the Old Accord. They call it 'the long hum'. I like theirs better. It implies we are still in the middle of it.
There is an old Shulkin proverb: 'Dine with a Chorrin only if you have nowhere to be.' I have not had anywhere to be since I met one.
At the Crossing there is a Chorrin who hums outside my window each closed hour. I never asked. I never thanked them. I leave a lamp lit on that side. I think it is all the thanks they want.
I have watched the Chorrin mourn. They gather and hum a single note all night while the crowns of the dead wilt. Afterwards nobody speaks of it. It is the opposite of a Shulkin closing, and as true.
A small Chorrin figure sits on my desk, carved from chorus root by a child. It has the wrong number of fingers and exactly the right expression. I have sat with it on bad nights.
When a Chorrin crown wilts with sorrow, the others tuck a sprig of their own into it. In the end it is a patchwork. Nothing is so honest. We write a letter. They give a piece of themselves.
9: My oldest friend was a Chorrin. They went quiet mid-hum, at a kiln, laughing at some joke of mine. I've never dared tell it again.
If you're ever in a Stead, tell them {name} of {village} sends formal regards. They'll know what that means. It means warm ones.
The Old Accord was more than trade. Our walls were their harvests; their songs had our lamps in them. I'd like to see that again before I close.
In the vault is a bundle labelled 'Chorrin Songs, Unsorted'. Nobody has read it in a century. I read it every closed hour. I understand no note and never stop weeping. Lid down, of course.
A Chorrin sprout calls me 'Elder Inkwell'. I have not corrected them. I am not sure which of us is being teased.
On the day I met my first Chorrin I wrote, 'We shall be friends, at some distance.' I keep that page for the pleasure of how wrong I was.
A Chorrin once asked whether the Archive would write them down when they closed. I said yes. They asked what it would say. I said, 'Loud.' They hummed a while. I have never been prouder of a word.
