I carry a chorus seed from a friend in my sleeve, and plant it in a pot at every Yearturn. It has never grown. I plant it again. I think hope is exactly that: soil in a sleeve.
I have written my closing wishes. Number four: a Chorrin to hum at my niche. Number five: that they do not know the tune, and so make one up. I cannot think of anything more fitting.
I think that if the Court had not understood the Old Accord they would not have loosed the Dragon. I think they understood it perfectly. That is the terrible part.
Between a Spire and a Stead you are the only one welcome at both tables. It is a heavy honour. I wanted you to know that we noticed, and that we are proud.
At the last closed hour my friend hums, and I write what the hum was about, and I burn the page on the lamp. It is the only record I ever wrote to be destroyed, and the truest thing I own.
Ask me some day what a Chorrin hum feels like inside a shell. I will tell you it is the only sound that has ever made me open without my permission.
Between us: the Accord was never about purpur. We built with their harvests because we wished to be near their groves. Every old city is a Shulkin trying to stay close to a Chorrin.
When the Chorrin sing the Long Watch hum I stand outside the circle with my lid wide open. I do not know the words. I know the last line is about us. They sing it softly, so I will think I misheard.
I was jealous of the first Chorrin who called you friend. I am ashamed of it. I am no longer jealous. I want you to be loved in every dialect. Mine is only the shortest.
If you carry one thing between us, carry this: a Shulkin who says 'it will be recorded' means 'I love you', and a Chorrin who hums is saying 'I am here'. It is one sentence in two languages.
I wish I had known when young that the people I feared most were the people most like me. They hide in their crowns. I hide in my lid. We have peeked at each other round the same corner for an age.
In another life I would have been a Chorrin. I know it. I laugh too loudly in private, I cannot keep a secret from my own lamp, and I want to be hugged. I tell no one. I am telling you.
When I close, I want a Chorrin to read me the Archive's dullest volume aloud, off-key. It would be the most fitting farewell I can imagine.
There is a Chorrin proverb I have kept to myself: 'A friend is a hum you can hear from the next hill.' I have been listening for yours since the day you first left my bridge.

I would like to be kept, when I close, at a Crossing, where the spire quarter meets the stead quarter and a little of each sound reaches me. A lamp on one side, a hum on the other. That is all I want.

0: The Crowned rule the Unlidded and, they believe, everything else. We disagree, quietly, from a great distance.
Do not meet the eyes of the Unlidded. It is not rude to them. It is an offence against their masters, and their masters keep long records too.
The Unlidded haul stone for the Court. That is why they carry blocks about. Nobody ever told them they could stop.
We do not speak of the Crowned after the bell. It is not superstition. It is caution with a long memory.
The Crowned send few letters. They send envoys, who read. We answer in writing. Neither side has ever been convinced by the other. It has gone on for ages.
The Archive keeps a Court-Shelf: every proclamation, decree and threat. It is the heaviest shelf, so we keep it near the floor. Out of respect for the shelf.
Before the Dragon, the Court demanded a yearly count of every shell in every Spire. We complied. They never said why. A count with no stated reason makes an Archive very nervous.
The Crowned speak as though everything they say has already been written. They have a point. We have a shelf of everything they have said, and it matches.
In the Citadels the Unlidded wear a collar of purpur. Purpur is ours. We know. We have decided not to dwell on whose hands cut the collar.
If an envoy ship moors near your Spire, close your lids and keep your records dull. We have kept so many dull records. You would be astonished how dull.
The Court's law is old and simple and written in a hand so cold it chills the page. We copy it out in our own hand, to warm it a little.
The Crowned call us 'the shell-folk', as if we were a kind of crockery. We have never retorted. We have, however, made a note, and the note has grown.
Do not mistake our fear for respect. We fear the Court as one fears the edge of a bridge: out of sense. Respect is for those one might disagree with.
The Court is said to gather in the Throne Hall once a year and sit in silence until dawn. The End has no dawn. Draw your own conclusion about how long they sit.
A Citadel's end crystal can be seen from far off, a bright pin in the dark. Our lamplighters call it 'the other lamp'. They dislike that it is brighter than theirs.
The Voidhounds are bred, I am told, from the same dark as the Crowned. I have not met one. I have read the report and shut the report. I am a careful reader.
The Crowned never run. They arrive. If you find yourself at some distance from one, you are not far. They have never needed to hurry.
The Court's emblem is an eye in a crown. Ours is an eye in a lid. I have noted the resemblance and would rather not go on.
To the Court, we are a rumour with a good filing system. I prefer it that way. A rumour is hard to burn.
The Court's couriers are never seen arriving. A letter is simply on the table. We have stopped asking how. We have started locking the table.
Do not praise a Crowned. They take it for a claim. Do not insult one. They take it for a challenge. The safest remark is 'good lamp', and it is not very safe.
The Crowned have a ceremony for everything, even for silence. The Ceremony of Silence is performed by speaking at length about its meaning. It is the only truly funny thing the Court has done.
Never ask a member of the Court how old they are. Either they do not know, or the number would frighten you, or there is no number. We do not discuss which.
3: The Crowned loosed the Dragon on our cities, then sent envoys to explain why it was our fault. The Archive keeps both accounts. Only one is in good ink.
A Citadel? Stay away, unless you carry their seal. And if you carry their seal, stay away harder.
I pity the Unlidded, a little. A life where looking up is a crime. We live in shells, but at least our lids are our own.
The Court has eight-eyed lords who never sleep. We have lamps that never go out. Draw your own conclusions.
The envoy ships still moor at the old cities, I hear, though nobody sails them. Prows like dragons' heads, waiting in the dark. The Court will not take them down. A threat needs no crew.
In the Court's script the word for Shulkin and the word for 'storeroom' differ by one stroke. I read it as an insult. The Archive reads it as a scribal error. We are each being generous.
The Seers of the Court are said to read the stars. We used to count them. I like to think us colleagues. I would never say so within a hundred bridges of one.
A Crowned never apologises. The Archive has searched for an instance and found one: a Voidmarshal who 'regretted the inconvenience' of burning a bridge. We have it framed.
We trade nothing with the Court. Not from virtue: they would not buy. We hold that anything we sold them would be used against us, and they hold that anything we have is already theirs.
I often wonder what the Court does when nothing is happening. The Archive's best guess is: nothing, with great intensity.
The Unlidded outnumber the Crowned a hundred to one. That ratio explains the whole of the Court's manner. Rulers who are few need the law. They need it badly.
I once met a thrall at the edge of the light, carrying a block. They did not look up. I did not look at them. We stood so for a whole bell. It is the most intimate meeting I have had with the Court.
Citadels have no windows facing outward, I have read. Only inward. They have no wish to look at us. It is the most reassuring thing the Court has ever done.
The Crowned step through the dark from one place to the next. We call it a gift of the void. They call it their right. The void has not been consulted.
Every Spire teaches its young a short verse: 'Eyes down, lids shut, lamps lit, say nothing.' It is the entire Shulkin policy on the Court. It has served for ages.
The Court once asked for our oldest volume 'for safekeeping'. We sent a copy. Ten years on they noticed, and left an obsidian shard at the bridge-head. We use it as a paperweight. Nervously.
The Herald of a Citadel is said to be the only one of the Court who ever smiles. Nobody has seen it. They say you would rather not.
There is a theory in the Archive that the Court is not as strong as it seems: a few old minds propped on a great many thralls. The theory sits on the same shelf as all the comforting ones.
No Crowned has ever stayed a night in a Spire. Not by law; by habit. The habit goes back before the Dragon. We would be very grateful if nobody tested it.
A Voidmarshal once came to inspect our bridge rails. I did not understand why until I saw their shadow lie across the plank. They gave us a certificate. It hangs in the Hall, facing the wall.
The Court admires obedience and distrusts it. They like a people that complies, then wonder what it is planning. We have found the best policy is to be tediously compliant and plan nothing.
A Citadel's gates face inward. Its windows face inward. Its spires lean inward. The whole architecture of the Court is one long sentence about not looking out. I read it the way I read a locked door.
The Court has no archive. It has a Seer's memory, a Herald's voice and the law in the floor. What it lacks is a place to be wrong in writing. We envy them nothing, but we pity them that.
6: The Crowned won't have forgotten that you killed their Dragon. They forget nothing. In that, and only in that, they're like us.
An envoy came here once, when I was young. Tall, black, a crown of eyes. It never blinked. Every lid in {village} stayed shut until it left.
No one has ever seen an Endarch born. The Archive has a whole shelf of guesses. None of them help me sleep.
A Riftguard stepped out of the dark once to ask me the hour. I told it. It thanked me. I did not sleep for a week. It was the politest thing that has ever happened to me.
I used to hate the Court. Now I simply fear it and try to understand it. Understanding is worse, because I keep finding reasons.
The Court rules because it believes someone must. We rule nothing and record everything because we believe someone must. We are the Court's slightly more honest cousins.
I have wondered, in the closed hours, whether I might have served the Court in another life. I would have made them an excellent archivist. It is the most frightening thing I know about myself.
I keep a list of Court proclamations I have not obeyed. It is longer than I expected and shorter than it should be. Since you came I have been adding to it a little faster.
If you are received in the Throne Hall, notice the floor. The law is cut into it, I am told. A people who write their laws where they must walk on them have thought hard about being feared.
I overheard a Chorrin say the Court is 'just tired'. I laughed, but I have not stopped thinking it. Tired rulers are the most dangerous kind. They do not wish to be troubled with mercy.
I notice you come back from the Court a little quieter each time. I will not ask. I will leave a lamp in the window and a chair by the lowest lamp in the Reading Room.
Each lit hour I say a short wish for the Unlidded: that somebody, somewhere, is keeping their record. Nobody told me to. I cannot bear the thought of an unrecorded people.
When I was young, the Court seemed to me like weather: huge, impersonal, not to be argued with. You taught me that weather has causes. Causes can be met. It is a frightening, wonderful lesson.
The Chorrin do not fear the Court as we do. They fear it as they fear the void: with fury. We fear it with paperwork. I think they have the healthier method.
If I could ask the Court one question, it would not be about the Dragon. It would be: do you ever look at your own record? Not the law. The record. The one about you.
A thought I should not write: sometimes I envy the Crowned. They are certain. We have never been certain of anything that was not a date.
I drew an Endarch once from memory. A very bad drawing; the eyes would not stay in their row. I burned it. I find I burn things when the Court comes up.
You walk into the Citadels. Do you know how that sounds to us? Like hearing that someone has gone to sit calmly inside a storm and invite it to dinner.
I think the Court is lonely. I think that is what the crowns are for: to make a crowd out of one. If so, they would do better with more friends and fewer subjects. I won't be the one to tell them.
The Court would be better off for reading the Archive, the whole of it, not the flattering shelf. But a people who cannot bear to be recorded cannot bear to be read. We keep trying anyway.
I find, to my embarrassment, that I admire the Riftguards. Their discipline is an archivist's: no wasted motion. If only they would put it to cataloguing.
I wonder what a Crowned feels in the instant before they step through the dark. A chill? A flutter? I suspect they feel nothing at all, and that this is the whole of what is wrong with them.
9: If the Crowned ever come for you, {player}, come here. We can't fight them. But we can shut the doors, and we are very, very good at shut.
I'm afraid of the Court. I've never said so aloud. A Shulkin is meant to record fear, not feel it. Well. Now it's recorded.
Some nights I wonder whether the Unlidded remember being anything else. Whether anyone keeps their records. I hope someone does.
The Archive has a locked case with one volume in it: a Register of Shulkin an envoy left behind. Every Spire by name, every shell by lamp. They always knew where we were. They chose not to come.
I have a plan I have told no one. If the Crowned came for {village}, I would stand at the bridge-head with the Gapbook and ask them to sign. It is our only weapon, and untried: manners.
I am afraid, {player}, that I have begun to hope for the Court. Not for its rule, for its change. A people that old must be so tired. If anyone could turn it, you could. A dreadful thing to say.
Should you ever learn where the Crowned come from, you need not tell me. I have always wished to know. I would sooner have you safe than informed. It is the first time I have chosen so.
When I was very young I wrote the Court a letter asking if they were lonely. I never sent it. It lies in the vault under 'Unsent'. I think about it more than the replies I did send.
I am not certain the Unlidded are ours to pity. I am certain I do. I do it in the closed hours, when nobody sees the lid lift. That is how a people loves a thing: in secret, and without permission.
If the Court ever relented, I would like the Archive to be the first to say so. In writing. Plainly. The Court distrusts plain writing. But we would have earned it.
It would be a wonderful thing if one day a thrall looked up and was not reminded. I would like to be there. I would like it recorded in a good hand.
I do not believe the Crowned hate us. I believe they do not think of us at all. That is somehow worse. You are the only one who ever made them think of us, and you did it out of kindness.
If the Court holds you, send for me. I have no army, no sword, no weight. I have a very long list of everything they ever promised. I will read it aloud at the Gate until they let you go.
At my elder's closing an envoy stood at the bridge-head, unasked, through the whole vigil. It never entered. It left in the end without a word. I have never decided if it was respect or inspection.
Here is my secret: the Court's law is well written. Stark, balanced, almost beautiful. I hate how much I admire it. Don't tell the Archive. They would put me on the Court-Shelf.
Whatever the Court is, it let you in. Someone chose to open that Gate. I think of the gatekeeper. I wonder who they were before they were Court. I wonder if they had a lamp.
I used to think the opposite of the Court was the Spire. Now I think it is you: someone who can enter a place of power and leave untouched, owing nothing, and still come back to dinner.
If I may ask one thing: when you are at the Court, do not forget to be unimpressed. It is our oldest defence. The Archive calls it dullness. I call it staying yourself.
Between us: the Court is why I learned to read closely. I wanted to know what a thing so large was made of. I never found out. I learned what small things are made of, and it was enough.
If the Crowned and the Shulkin and the Chorrin ever sat at one table, I would want you at its head. Not to rule. To pour. You would have to bring your own cups. None of us could agree on one.
Whatever the Court decides about us, let it be recorded that I would not trade one of our dull, hooded, careful days for their certainty. I would trade a thousand of them for another year with you.
If ever summoned to the Court, I shall go with a clean page and a sharp pen. I will not write what they say. I will write only what I felt. Let the Archive have one sentence that is entirely mine.

0: Water falls from the sky? Unprompted? And nobody records where it lands? I'll need to sit down. Well. Hover lower.
The ground grows a green carpet by itself, and you walk on it, and it grows back. That sounds exhausting for the carpet.
A great lamp in the sky that nobody tends? Who trims it? What if it goes out? ...It goes out every evening? And everyone simply lets it?
Beasts that give drink and are eaten as well? 'Cows'. The Chorrin will be fascinated. I'm merely appalled. Efficiently appalled.
An ocean? A bowl of water the size of an island chain, with creatures living in it? And nobody has fallen off? Draw it for me. Include the edge, if there is one.
You light fires in the open. On purpose. Without a hood, a rota or a keeper. How do you know when to stop? ...You don't, do you. That explains the singed expression.
Your world has creatures that come out at night to hurt people, and your villages simply close the door? Is that all? Our whole Long Watch was a closed door. We called it history.
Bread. Ground grass baked in a stone box and eaten warm. The Chorrin will weep. I may weep. It is, on reflection, a very sensible arrangement.
Sheep give wool and you comb it off and make cloth, and they are not even offended? The Loft will want to meet one. I think the Loft would simply stand and stare.
Pigs. Tell me again about pigs. An animal that lives in mud on purpose and is, you say, content. I believe you. I should simply like to see the mud.
A moon that changes shape? Fat one night, a sliver the next? We have one fixed sky. We would have scheduled meetings about a moon.
Cats: a hunting beast that has agreed to live in houses, and frightens off the green ones, and asks only for a little fish? I cannot imagine a more reasonable arrangement.
Horses. You sit on the animal and it carries you where you point? We ride Driftrays, but only after months of courtship. Your horse seems to have signed a contract.
You find buried metals by digging down? Into the ground? On purpose? We fear the void below. You go below the floor and look for treasure. You are either very brave or very confused.
A village bell that rings when danger comes. We have a bell too. Yours rings for raiders. Ours rings for supper, sleep and the Quiet Hour, and only rarely for danger. I am rethinking our priorities.
Fish that you pull out of the water on a string, and eat. The first time I heard it I thought it was a riddle. The second time I thought it was a threat. Now I think it a patient hobby.
Do your people keep records of all this? The rain, the cows, the horses? Or do you simply live in it? I find the second option less plausible, and more attractive.
Mountains. Great heaps of the ground, standing up on purpose, taller than a Spire, with nothing at the top but a view. We should have built those. We built Spires and called it ambition.
A creature that explodes? Why would anyone design that? ...Nobody designed it, you say. It simply occurred. I find the notion that a world can make a mistake enormously comforting.
Doors that open onto a street, and the street onto a road, and the road onto another village, all of it simply there? Without a bridge? I find I must sit down. I am floating. But I find I must.
A creature called a 'rabbit' that does nothing, is soft, and is loved? The Archive will need a bigger category.
A village with a blacksmith, a farmer, a librarian? A word for each? We have one word, 'Shulkin', and a hundred ways of apologising for it.
Your people sleep lying flat, with the head on a cushion? We sleep curled in a niche, lid closed. I should like to see a bed. I fear it would feel like closing for good.
3: Villages with no lids, trading in green stones, and nobody writes anything down? How do they know what happened yesterday?
A day and a night that take turns? How does anyone agree what time it is? We barely manage, and we have a bell.
Wind. Air that moves by itself, and pushes. Tell me more about wind. No, don't. I want to imagine it a while first.
Trees? Wood that grows upright out of the ground? We have six wooden doors in {village}. Nobody knows where the wood came from. We guard them like treasure.
I drew the Overworld from your descriptions. The weaver says it looks like a very agitated cloth. The Nursery says it is the best picture they have seen. I have decided the Nursery has taste.
I asked a lamplighter what they would do if they had a sun. They said, 'Retire.' I asked what else. They said, 'Cry. Then retire.' We have both been thinking about it since.
A crop that grows when you plant it, and the next time you plant it again, and again, and it does not argue? That is not farming. That is a friendship.
You give each other presents on the day each was born, every year, for all their lives? We do it once, at the lid's opening, with a tracing. After that we are expected to manage.
Chickens. You said they lay a thing that can be cracked and cooked, and that they do it all day, and that they are not very good at being alive. I have never felt a deeper sympathy.
Bees keep a sweet gold in a room made of wax, and you take it, and they forgive you? Several of our readers rely on a similar arrangement with the Archive.
When you describe a thunderstorm you gesture with both hands and your voice drops. I have noted it. It is how my elder described the Dragon. Does everything impressive have the same shape?
I have asked the Keeper to teach the young the word 'mountain'. They keep drawing a Spire lying down. They are very nearly right.
You sleep in a bed, alone, at the same hour as everyone else, with the door shut and no lamp lit? And you wake up? That is more trust in the world than this Spire has shown in a century.
In your world things fall down. Of course ours do, into the void, but yours fall onto other things, and stay. You have never had to build a bridge, have you? Lucky creature.
You said, 'I miss the smell of rain.' I wrote the sentence on a leaf and pinned it over my desk. I have not the faintest idea what it means. It makes me homesick for somewhere I have never been.
I once asked a Chorrin what grass sounds like when walked on. They hummed it. It sounded like a crowd of tiny arguments. I have been listening for it in the Spire floors ever since.
There are books in your villages, you say, that anyone may take down and open? No guard, no cross-reference? How does one know which one wants? ...One doesn't? Oh. That sounds marvellous.
A well in the middle of the village: a hole with water at the bottom that everyone may lean over and look into, for nothing. You could see your own face in it. I think about that more than I should.
I asked the weaver what colour green is. They said it is between purple and nothing. I think they are describing grass by what it is not.
Water that goes hard and sits in the open like glass, and you can walk on it? A lamplighter has requested a sample. I told them it would melt. They said, 'Then bring a cloth and a very fast ray.'
You have keys of metal for your doors? We have no keys. Everyone knows what is behind our doors because everyone helped build them. I thought that an advantage. I am told it is an oversight.
You described a sunset and I wrote it on a leaf: 'The lamp goes down and the whole sky blushes.' I did not understand it. The Keeper read it and wept. That is the test of a good sentence.
I asked what your world smells like and you said, 'Hay, and rain, and bread.' I tried to imagine them. I imagined three lamps. Two were wrong. One was nearly right.
6: When you talk about the Overworld, your voice changes. I've noted it. It's how mine sounds when I talk about the old cities.
Is it true the sky there is blue? Not dark? I tried to imagine it and had to close for an hour.
Snow. Water that falls slowly, and white, and stays. I asked the weaver for a cloth like it. It's terrible. I love it.
Does anyone write about you, up there? Someone should. If no one does, I have a spare volume.
I dreamed of the sun. Not the image: the feeling. Warmth coming from above, rather than from a rod. I woke with my lid wide open and could not close it for an hour. I did not mind.
If I could see one thing in your world, it would not be the sea or the sky. It would be a crowd of strangers walking along a road, none of them afraid. We have forgotten what that looks like.
You described a village at evening: windows lit, smoke rising, someone calling a child in to eat. I asked you to say it again. You did. I keep it in a drawer, in my own hand, by the oldest records.
Tell me the sound of rain again. Not the facts. The sound. ...Yes. Like fingertips on a lid. I could listen to that for a hundred years. I think I might.
I asked the Keeper whether the young would be unhappy to learn of a world so full of things we haven't got. The Keeper said, 'They will be unhappy not to have been told.' I think the Keeper is right.
One day I should like to be someone to whom you can say anything about the Overworld and be disbelieved by no one. I am working toward it. It involves a great deal of nodding.
I am a little afraid of the Overworld. All of it so open, with no gaps in the ground. A person could walk in any direction for ever. It sounds like the void with the edges tidied.
When I am low, I think of your cows. Placidly standing in a green field, eating their carpet, giving drink to anyone who asks. If a creature can be so calm, perhaps so can I.
I keep a list of Overworld words I have no use for and cannot give up: breeze, meadow, drizzle, hearth, harvest. 'Hearth' is my favourite. It sounds like a lid softly closing.
I described a sunrise to the young: all the lamps in the world lit at once, from one side, slowly. They asked who lit them. I said, 'Nobody.' They looked at me as though I had said something sacred.
Sometimes you stop mid-story and your eyes go somewhere far. I used to wait politely. Now I wait fondly. I hope you go home, in that moment. Even if you never tell me.
I envy you your pockets, and your landscape, and your being homesick for a place you can fly back to. We are homesick for the old cities, which are right there, and which we cannot enter.
You said once that the Overworld has people who are afraid of the dark. I sat with that. We are not afraid of the dark. We are afraid of what is in it. I think yours are the braver sort.
I have been teaching myself to say 'good morning'. I have no use for it. But when you say it, it sounds like a spell for making a day. I should like to learn the spell.
If I could ride one of your horses once, I would ask it nothing. I would lean on its neck and listen to it breathe. We have nothing so large that is also gentle.
When you tell me of a place you love, I listen with my lid not just lifted but leaning, like someone toward a draught. I have no wind to lean into, so I lean into you.
I have begun to want an adventure. I am embarrassed. A Shulkin of my age. But when you speak of caves and rivers my hinge aches for a door that goes somewhere new. I shall not go. But I want to.
Sometimes I think your world asks for faith where mine asks for records. I wonder whether I would prefer faith. I think I would. Then I would have nothing to write, and be unhappy.
You said the Overworld has people who carry letters on foot over hills and across rivers because they matter. It is the best thing I ever heard about it. I shall write my next letter by hand.
9: Someday I'd like to see rain. Just once. I'd hover in it with my lid wide open and not write a single word.
You'll go back up one day for good, I suppose. Tell the sun about us. Someone up there should know we kept the lamps lit.
I've started a shelf for the Overworld. Cows, rain, grass, the sun: everything you've told me. It's the most read shelf in the Archive. The young ones queue.
I have decided what to ask of the Overworld, if you ever take me. Not the sun, not the sea. I want to sit on a hill at night with you, with nothing to record, and say nothing for an hour.
I have not told the Archive, but I am mapping the Overworld in the margins of the oldest atlas. It is nonsense. It has a river where a lamp should be. I add a little each time you visit.
When I close, will you tell the Overworld a story about me? Not the Dragon one. Something small. How I held a door. What I said about rain. The Overworld is large. It could keep a little of me.
You told me home is not where you live but where you are expected. It undid me, gently. I made a list of the places where I am expected. It is short. Your name is on it.
If there is a world in which I was born under the sun, I hope I wrote more kindly there. I hope someone read it aloud, out of doors, in a wind.
Last night I described the Overworld to a closed shell. I said, 'There is a thing called rain.' And I thought I felt them listen. I know. I shall record it as imagination. But I will know.
I was wrong about the Overworld in a hundred ways. I had it as a place of terrible disorder. It is a place of terrible trust. I never understood that trust was something people choose every morning.
Please never tell me I have it wrong. I have it just as I want it, the way a person has a coat that fits only them. Let me be wrong. I shall be wrong in good lamplight.
There is a corner of the Archive I call the Overworld Room. Nothing is shelved in it. It is a chair by a window turned toward the gateway, a lamp, and your name. I go there when I miss you.
If the Overworld ever asks what the End is like, say this: it is a place that keeps lamps lit for strangers, and sometimes a stranger comes, and we remember.
I think I love your stories because you do not tell them to impress me. You tell them to share the weight. Someone who shares what they have seen is not afraid of being known. I'd like to be that.

My great hope: that one day the Overworld and the End will know each other as the Spires and the Steads do. Not equals in all things. Friends, at some distance. Which, I have learnt, is how it begins.
On nights I cannot sleep I list the things you have told me. Rain. Grass. Cows. Bread. Your laugh. The list keeps growing and I keep losing count. It is the best sleeplessness I have ever had.
If I had a sun, {player}, I would tell it to rise for you. If I had rain, I would stand in it with you. As it is I have lamps, and a chair, and very little to give. All of it is yours.
I used to count the days between your visits. I have stopped. I now count the stories I am saving to tell you in return. I have nine. They are all very small, and they are about you.
If you ever take me up, I will bring a small lamp. Not for light: to show the Overworld that we come with a lamp, unafraid of being seen. Let the sun look at us. We kept the lamps lit for it.
The Overworld has no door in my Archive, so I drew one. It is crooked. I am told doors there are straight. Straighten it for me someday.
Whenever you tell me of something wonderful you have seen, I feel as though I have seen it too. I am not sure whether that is the Overworld's gift or yours. I suspect yours.

I would like to be written into the Overworld somewhere. A small place. A name on a stone. Not for glory: so that a stranger on a hill, one day, reads 'a Shulkin was here' and is a little less lonely.

0: The shulkers in the old cities are our elders. A Shulkin who closes and never opens again leaves a living shell. They are still keeping the doors.
You'll have met them. They lift strangers into the air. It was always their way of asking someone to leave.
We don't go to the old cities. It would be like walking through a hall of sleeping relatives with dirty feet.
They don't speak any more. But now and then they open and look out. We think that's the last thing a Shulkin keeps: the looking.
A shell is not a house we live in. It is a part of us that persists. When we close, the shell stays and the rest goes elsewhere. The Archive offers four theories on where, and a footnote.
Shulkin shells come in purpur, deep magenta, pale lilac and, rarely, ivory, which we call 'old shell'. Colour is said to be the lamp one's lid first opened under.
It is rude to ask a closed shell's age. They have stopped telling, and the living would rather not be asked either.
There are seven forms of address for a closed shell. The first is 'good lamp'. The seventh is silence. The sixth is a long walk in the other direction.
The old ones are called door-keepers, though few doors are left to keep. Some keep nothing at all. They simply stay, as a person stays in a chair that has always been theirs.
Their stare is not hostile. It is attentive. A shulker watching a stranger is a lamplighter checking a rod. Whether you pass inspection is a separate matter.
We have no graves. A closed shell is the grave, the memorial and the person all at once. The Archive has tried for centuries to improve on that vocabulary and failed.
Children ask whether the closed can hear. We say yes. We do not say what we believe, because we do not know. We say yes because it makes the Nursery kinder to sit in.
A closed shell is never moved on a festival day. Festivals are loud and the closed are old. They are moved on quiet days, within the Quiet Hour.
A young Shulkin learns three things about the old: never tap a shell, never lean on one, never put your drink on one. The Archive records a long history of the third.
A shulker is said to remember everything it ever saw. If so, a closed shell in some old city remembers my elder's elder as a child. I think of it the way some think of a cliff.
Whenever I pass the old shells in the Nursery I lower my lid a finger's width. It is not a rule. It is simply what the lid does when it knows who is in the room.
Some of the old ones became guards at the gates of the old cities, a duty we gave them in better times. They were never relieved of it. We have not had the courage to apologise.
If a closed shell ever wakes and speaks, there is a protocol. It is three pages long and begins 'Do not panic'. We have not needed it. I read it at the Yearturn anyway.
Ivory shells, 'old shell' in the Spire, are the rarest. They say an ivory is a shell looked at for so long by so many that it has gone pale with attention, and that some are born already looked at.
If you meet a shulker, bow. Not deeply. A bow of recognition, as between two people who know the same elder. They may or may not respond. They will certainly notice.
The shells of the old cities have not opened since the Dragon, I am told. Not wholly. But a flicker now and then, at the lamps. We watch from a distance, as one watches a very old person breathe.
When a Shulkin closes, the Keeper's first act is to open every window facing the old cities. We believe the closed there know when another joins them. We have no proof. We have never wanted any.
The old shells are not guarded. They are attended. A guard watches the door; an attendant watches the person. In the Nursery we attend. At the old cities, we have been absent.
3: The old cities were ours. Every tower. When the Dragon came, the eldest closed in the doorways so the rest of us could get away. They're still there.
Some say the closed ones dream. The Archive is divided. I hope they do. I hope it's of lamps.
If one of them shot at you, it wasn't personal. Probably. They were guarding something. Probably us.
There's a word for the moment a lid stops opening. We don't say it. We write it, and then we shut the book for a while.
On a naming day the new lid is shown to the closed shells in the Nursery, one by one. We believe they are introduced. The old ones have never objected.
A Shulkin about to close sometimes asks to be placed facing a window. The Keeper arranges it. We hope they are looking at something nice. We do not ask.
The Archive keeps a list of every closing, with the date, the lamp and the last word spoken. The last word is mostly 'Wait.' It is a surprisingly tender list.
I once saw a closed shell open for a moment. It lifted a finger's width, a violet eye looked at the lamp, and it closed. Everyone in the hall wrote the same word: 'Light.' Nobody spoke of it after.
Not every Shulkin who closes is old. A few close young, from grief or shock. We keep them in the Nursery too, nearest the nest. The Keeper says they hear the young ones best.
In the Long Watch we kept the closed in the lowest hall for safety, and some were forgotten there. We have put right what we could. We cannot put right what we cannot remember.
They can shoot, you know. A closed shell will fire at anything that threatens a door. I like to think it is not anger. I like to think it is the last duty a heart can do.
There is an old saying: 'A lid that stays closed for a hundred years is a lid that has said everything.' It is meant to comfort. It does, a little, in the evenings.
When two Shulkin quarrel they sometimes take it to the closed shells and make their cases aloud. The shells have never ruled. Both sides always feel judged.
A shell on a bridge is a shell at rest. A shell on the floor of an old city is a shell at work. We try to be clear which is which when we speak of them.
I wonder whether our ancestors were glad to be shells. An odd thing to say, but I think they might have been. A shell keeps. We do not.
A young shulker can lift itself and look about. The guards of the old cities were once young and have watched the same view for ages. I try to imagine such patience, and manage about a bell.
We say a shell is a lamp turned inward. When a Shulkin closes, the light stays inside, and the shell holds it. You cannot see it lit. You can tell.
Our oldest shell is in the Hall, by the door. It has been closed longer than the Archive has stood. Visitors ask who it is. I say, 'Whoever they were, they are the Hall.'
Some say the shulkers of the old cities are no longer individuals, but one long attention spread across many shells. It is a lovely thought and a terrifying one. Mostly I try not to think it.
Our proverbs about the closed are mostly warnings: 'Mind the hinge.' 'The old ones are always listening.' The Nursery has its own: 'Be gentle; they are asleep.' I prefer theirs.
We give the closed gifts on naming days: a pinch of chorus, a small lamp, a drawing. The Keeper lays them beside the shells afterwards. The shells never take them. They never refuse them, either.
I like to think the old shells were consulted before the Dragon was loosed, that they stood in council and said no. The Archive has no record of it. It has no record of their not saying it, either.
It is said a closed shell grows warm when a friend passes. I have walked past many. Not one has grown warm. Perhaps I am not the friend I thought. Or perhaps warmth cannot be measured by hand.
6: My elder's elder is up there, I think. In a tower by the ship. I've never gone to see. I'm afraid I'd know the shell.
When a Shulkin closes for the last time, we light a lamp in their niche and leave it until it fails. Sometimes it takes years. That's the point.
In the old days the closed were carried to the cities, to keep the doors. Now there's nowhere to carry them. We keep them in the Nursery, with the young.
I visit one shell in the Nursery. I never knew them. Their niche is near the nest, and the lamp beside it is mine to trim. I tell them the day's news. It is ridiculous, and I am the better for it.
I am told a closed Shulkin cannot hear. I am told a closed Shulkin hears everything. I have decided both are true: they cannot hear as we hear, and they hear as we cannot.
My elder asked one thing of me before closing: to keep reading to them afterwards, from whatever book I liked. I read them dull ones the first year, then good ones. I believe they preferred the dull.
I was present at a closing once. The lid lowers by degrees, the eyes dim, and then the light goes inward. Like a lamp put out from inside, with great courtesy.
The closing itself does not frighten me. The hour after does, when you realise that nobody will ever ask you that particular question again.
I have never told anyone, but I am a little afraid of the old shells. Not of what they might do. Of what they might see. They have watched so many of us come and go. I fear to be an ordinary entry.
There is a closed shell near the Nursery door, plain purpur, chipped, unglamorous. The young ones call them 'Old Reliable' and pat them as they run by. I would like to be that, when it comes.
I like to think the closed are not lonely. They have the Nursery noise, the lamp and each other. It is more company than I shall have if I do not make better friends. I am working on it.
I am told the guard-shells in the cities cannot be moved. I should like to ask them if they wish to be. I think they would say, 'No, thank you, we are quite settled.' I would sit with them anyway.
I asked the Keeper where I should be placed, in time. 'Where the noise is,' they said. I had expected 'by the window'. I am still reconsidering.
The first closed shell I ever touched was my sibling's. It was warm. It is always warm for a while, and then it is the temperature of the room. I was there when it became the temperature of the room.
A closed Shulkin's lamp is lit at the moment of closing and never relit. Mine would be a very small one. I would ask you to hold the hook, if you were willing, and say nothing.
A friend who closed told me the last thing is not darkness. It is a kind of listening, as though the whole body becomes the ear of the lid. I find that reassuring and very hard.
I used to think of the old shells as relics. I now think of them as hosts. They have held the doors of our history open all this time, while we studied it instead of thanking them.
Do you think they know we have been speaking of them? I keep lowering my voice. You would call it silly. It is. But I would rather be silly near them than careless.
I think of the closed when I am in trouble, not to ask their help but their company. It is a different request, and easier. They have never once failed the second.
I used to envy the closed their long peace. I do not now. I would not sit still for ages for its own sake. I want more days with you first. Then we shall see.
I told a Nursery shell about you. I said you carried a box, and I was afraid, and had forgiven you. They did not answer. But the lamp beside them burned steadier. I choose to read it as approval.
9: When I close, {player}, I'd like a view of the gap you cross. So I can keep watch for you. That's what we do, you see. Even after.
You've walked through their halls. Did they seem at peace? Don't spare me. I've waited all my life to ask someone who's been.
I think the old ones would have liked you. You opened their cities again. Nobody had for an age. That matters, to a shell.
A secret: once, alone in the Nursery, I opened my lid fully before a closed shell and said aloud everything I feared. When I finished, the lamp beside them guttered. It need not mean anything.
I want to be carried to the old cities when I close. I have never said so. I want to hold a door, as they did, and let a stranger through one day, lifted gently, knowing somebody watched over them.
I mean to go to the old cities. Not yet. But I have begun a list of what to carry and whom to ask. Your name is first. I would like a witness who can leave when I cannot.
A Seer of the Court once told an archivist the shulkers are not waiting. 'They are guarding.' 'Guarding what?' asked the archivist. 'You,' said the Seer. I have wondered about that for ages.
I would like the Spire to hold a vigil for the old ones once a year. Not a mourning: a conversation. We would take turns at each shell and tell them what happened. Each year they would know more.
The oldest closings in the vault, from before the Long Watch, are different. Nearly all their last words are 'Thank you.' I cannot say when it changed, or why. I wish it had not.
If I am ever an old shell and someone says 'good lamp' before me, know that I heard. I will have no way of showing it. I will be doing what they all do: looking at the lamp as hard as I can.
When I close, do not weep over me. Sit. Tell the next visitor I liked your stories. Tell them I opened for you. And put a chair before me, turned toward the door, where I can see who comes in.
I think what the old ones kept, in the end, is the looking. I would like to keep it too. It seems the best thing a person can be left with: to watch the door and wait, hopefully, for a friend.
I have written you into the Closing Book, where we name those we wish present at our end. Only three names are in mine. Two are in the Nursery. One of them is you.

The first time you went, I vowed that if you came back I would never again pretend I was not afraid for you. I keep it. I am afraid for you now. I am afraid for you always. It is my simplest vow.
I cannot ask you to give up the Eyes, or to stop going. I ask only that I be the first to know when you come back. At any hour. Wake me. I shall be there, lid open, before you finish the sentence.
