If I'm honest, which the dark invites, I was never only lighting the village. I was lighting a path for someone to come home along. I just didn't know it would be you.
Odd: the rods burn exactly as they always did, and yet {village} seems brighter when you are in it. I've checked the sockets twice.
There are four hundred and twelve lamps in {village}, and not one of them can do what your knock on my door does. It's ridiculous. I wouldn't trade it.
I'll teach you the lamp-knots one day. They're a lamplighter's secret. Not that I'm sworn to it; it's just that nobody has ever asked.
When you're far away I stand at the top of the Tower, look the way you went, and say 'steady'. Like a rod. I've begun to mean it.
I used to count the dark. Years of it. Then you walked in carrying more light than I have ever managed, and I stopped counting. The dark didn't end. I just have company now.
Come up when you can. Not for the view. For the quiet, and the humming, and the sound of someone else breathing in a place that's been mine alone for a century.

0: Void-cloth comes off the looms up in the Loft. Robes, mantles, banners. It drinks light and gives back a little shimmer, like the gaps between stars.
I'm the {job}. That's my banner on the drying loft. The purple one. They're all purple. Mine is the correct purple.
Every robe in {village} came off my loom. I know everyone's measurements. I know secrets I'd rather not.
Don't step on the thread. It isn't fragile. It's that I'll know.
Nine hundred threads to a hand's width: that is void-cloth. If you can see through it, it's a failure. If it looks back at you, it's a masterpiece.
The Loft smells of cold dye and old lamplight. Don't breathe too deeply. I did once, and spent a week dreaming in violet.
Never fold void-cloth sharply. It remembers the fold, and every robe it becomes is creased in the same corner of the shoulder, for ever.
Robes in {village} are cut by hand, never by rule. A rule would make us all one shape. We are all reasonably different shapes, and would like to be admired for it.
I'm the {job} in {village}, and I count my days in rows. A good day is sixty rows. A bad day is the same sixty rows, undone.
My shuttle is a sliver of purpur, worn thin by centuries of hands. It slides like a sentence you have said many times.
We use three dyes: violet, violet, and a violet I'm not permitted to describe. They are all quite different. The Archive keeps swatches.
Dyed thread hangs to dry along the long bridge. When all the colours are out, it looks like a banner for a festival nobody has invented yet. Do watch your head.
Pins are forbidden in the Loft. We use thorns from the chorus stalk. They leave a little bloom behind, and the cloth smells faintly of chorus ever after.
A weaver's hands are slightly purple for life. A weaver's temper is slightly purple too. The two go together.
If your robe frays, bring it to me before the fray reaches the hem. A hem that gives way at a festival is a story the whole Spire tells for a decade.
3: The Eye of the Spires on our mantles takes nine passes. Nine. Young weavers weep at pass six. I wept at pass four.
Robes are cut long so nobody sees our feet. Nobody needs to see our feet. Our feet are the least dignified part of us.
I'm weaving a banner for the Lid Hall: the Old Accord, a lid and a chorus flower meeting. The Chorrin have asked for more flower.
The thread comes from all sorts of places. Some of it, honestly, I couldn't tell you. The loom doesn't mind.
The young ones come to the Loft to learn knots. There are fifty-one. They learn them all, forget them all, and then weave something lovelier by accident.
A robe for a naming is white, for a closing violet, for a quarrel brown. I've never woven a brown. I keep the thread anyway, in case.
Weaving is arithmetic with patience. A pattern is only a count that someone remembered to write down. I'm half an archivist and I deny it.
I once wove the Eye of the Spires into my own mantle backwards, by mistake. It's the one I wear to festivals. Several people think it's the correct way. I let them.
The warp threads sing if you strum them. I strum the loom only when I'm certain nobody is listening. The Loft hums for a whole lit span afterwards.
Chorrin cloth is looser, warmer, full of knots they leave in on purpose. I said 'sloppy' once. A Chorrin said 'alive'. We are both still thinking.
I hang a small woven eye above the Nursery nest. No stitch is pulled tight, so it moves a little in the draught of a sleeping lid. It's my favourite thing I make, and nobody notices.
Some of our thread comes unspun from robes in the old cities. Reuse isn't disrespect. It's a long conversation with the dead, conducted in thread.
Colour fades near the lamps. I weave a tone slightly too dark, so it matures into correctness. Planning ahead is just weaving with more patience.
I check every robe that comes back to the Loft for the places it was loved most. The elbows, mostly. You can read the past in an elbow.
Do keep still while I measure. I'm not being insulting. One of your shoulders sits a finger lower than the other. It's endearing, and a nightmare to cut for.
6: I wove my first robe for my elder. They wore it to rags, and then they closed in it. Still the best thing I ever made.
Could I measure you? For the record. I'd like to make you something. With sleeves that fit those odd little arms.
When I weave, I think about nothing at all. It's the only time. The rest of the time I'm Shulkin and I think about everything.
I hide a thread of my own colour in every banner. Nobody's found one yet. You may look, if you like.
I weave better when I'm worried and worse when I'm happy. It's most inconvenient. I'm told it's a common failing among those who make things.
The cloth that took longest was a wrap for a soft shell that never opened. Forty rows a day, for a month. I didn't know how else to carry it.
Sometimes I weave one row in a colour nobody asked for. It ends up inside a hem where only the wearer will ever know. I think of it as a small blessing.
I've never told the Lid Hall this: I was nearly a wayfinder. I wove nets for the Roost instead, and found that thread could carry me anywhere. Slower. Without the falling.
Weavers say: pull a thread and the whole village comes with it. I think it's about the Spire. It could just as well be about a sleeve.
Once I wove a single row from threads pulled out of everyone's hems in {village}. It looked like nothing. It looked like all of us. I have never undone it.
I see people by their cloth: the worn elbows, the pulled cuffs, the way a hem sits. You can read a whole life if you know how. Yours says: always moving.
A knot is a decision. Everything unfinished in {village} I can feel in some knot or other. Mine I leave loose on purpose. Closing is easier with loose ends.
The Chorrin dye from flowers and are cheerful about it. We dye from ground amethyst and are solemn about it. The colour is the same. The mood isn't.
My elder wove in silence. I weave talking. The loom doesn't mind either way, but I think the cloth I make while talking is warmer. The cloth I make alone is truer.
When you came in with that torn sleeve I nearly fainted. It wasn't the sleeve. It was that you had come back, and I would have something to mend.
9: I'm making you a mantle. It's not done; it never is. When you're far away, I add a row. It's getting rather long.
If I close before it's finished, take the loom. Not to use. Just so it goes somewhere it's loved.
The cloth I'm proudest of has a tiny flaw near the hem. I left it in. It's where I was laughing at something you said.
Your Overworld colours, the green and the sky's blue. I've been trying to dye them. My hands are blue to the wrist. Worth it.
I've been unpicking my best banner to reuse the thread for you. Don't look so alarmed. It's a good banner. You are a better reason.
There's a thread of Overworld green in the lining of the mantle I'm making you. I won't say where I found it. You know where. Don't tell the Archive I took a leaf.
A weaver weaves what they can't say. I've made you eleven things. Laid out in order, they can be read. They say: stay a little longer.
I'm teaching myself a Chorrin knot, the one that isn't tight and isn't loose. It's meant to hold a friend in place without holding them back. Mine keeps coming undone. It may be the right knot.
My last cloth will be a plain banner. No eye, no emblem, just the colour you looked at longest in the Loft. I've been watching.
A robe I made hangs by the Loft door in case you come in cold. I've altered the length twice, in case you grew. You haven't. I'm delighted.
I weave faster now. I worked out why. It isn't skill. I'm weaving toward something: the next time you walk in and ask, 'what are you making?'
If I could weave one thing, it would be the sound of your knock on the Loft door. I've tried six patterns. Four come out as rain. I've never heard rain, but I'm sure.
You needn't wear anything I make. It's so that I know you're warm. That's the whole reason anyone sews anything for anyone.
When you're away the Loft is exactly the same, every bobbin in its place, and it feels half-woven. I never knew a room could feel like that.
The finest thing in the Loft is a single strand of void-silk, so fine it can't be seen. I've been saving it for something that deserves it. I think I am nearly there.

0: I cut purpur and mend shells: buildings and people both, though I only charge the buildings.
Purpur is popped chorus, pressed and cut. Every block you've walked on was a Chorrin harvest once. Mind your manners on the bridges.
I'm the {job}. If something in {village} cracks, I hear it first. Usually because it cracks on my bench.
Stonecutters are loud. I've been deaf on one side of my shell for forty years. Speak up on my left.
My chisels are cut from amethyst. Iron is too blunt for purpur, and bone is too sentimental. Amethyst has the right opinion about everything.
A hinge is the hardest joint in the Spire. It must be strong enough to bear weight and loose enough to open at a breath. The two demands fight. I referee.
I measure a ledge with my eye and a bridge with my feet. If the two disagree, I trust the feet. The eye wants to be impressed.
No mortar. Purpur sits on purpur, held by its own weight and good manners. We copy the old cities, who copied the shells.
A cracked block rings flat when you tap it. A sound block rings like a small bell. I tap everything. People find it unnerving. People find falling walls more so.
Please don't lean on the unfinished arch. It looks finished. It is lying.
I'm the {job} in {village}. I keep a bench, a bucket of grey resin and forty-one chisels. I have named none of them, which I consider a mark of professional restraint.
Purpur dust gets everywhere. I've found it in my lid, my niche and, once, in the sleeping shell next door. A very faint violet, ever after.
Stairs are ceremonial. We glide, but a stair tells a visitor where the building thinks you ought to pause. I put a landing wherever a view wants admiring.
A pillar should lean, very slightly, toward what it holds up, the way a good listener leans toward a speaker. Straight pillars are for the Court.
I plane every block with the grain, wipe it with a cloth, and tell it what it's for. Say that to a Chorrin and they hum for an hour. Say it to a Shulkin and they write it down.
3: A cracked lid is a terrible thing. I patch them with resin and patience. Mostly patience. The resin runs out.
Everything here echoes a shell: a body, a gap, a lid. I didn't design it. I simply refuse to build anything else.
Bring me a broken block and I'll tell you its story. Bring me a broken shell and I'll tell you to sit down and hold still.
Purpur pillars are cut along the grain. Yes, it has a grain. No, nobody believes me until they've ruined a pillar.
There is a way to cut a corner so it looks sharp from the front and gentle from the side. It took me forty years. It's called 'the courtesy'.
The first thing I ever carved was a lid for a toy. Awful. Lopsided. It's still on my bench. It reminds me what I'm for: making shells people can be happy in.
A chip in a pillar isn't a flaw. It's a record. The Archive has lost a lot of nuance by insisting I fill them in.
The old cities' joins are so fine that not even void-silk will pass between them. In ours, a finger of cloth slips through. We're improving. We'll match them in about three hundred years.
Careful on the lower arch. It's the oldest in {village}. It has held for six hundred years, and I would like it to hold six hundred more without the weight of a shocked look.
Mending a shell is simple. You clean the break, press the edges together, and wait. The waiting is the cure. It's why shellwrights make such patient company.
The Steads make better resin than we do. The Chorrin boil it with a single chorus petal. I told them I'd steal the secret. They told me the secret. It is a petal. I feel foolish.
In every building I leave one block a little rough, hidden at the back. It's where the building keeps its opinions.
Every window in the Spire is cut a hair off-square. Square windows make the eye feel judged. I won't tell you which corner.
Sometimes I build a staircase that goes nowhere, purely as a pause. The young ones race up it, stand on the top step, and look at where they might have gone. Best work I do.
I tested a bridge once by walking its whole span. Halfway I realised I had started apologising to it. The bridge held. I now apologise on all bridges.
6: I mended my own lid once, after a fall. In a mirror. Badly. That's the dent you're too polite to look at.
The old cities were built by shellwrights like me. Better than me. I've seen their joins. I'd give a hand to learn them. I'd manage with the other.
When a young one's shell first hardens, I check the hinge. They always flinch. I always say it's fine. It almost always is.
I built every bridge rail in {village}. I check each one every year. People think I'm fussy. People haven't fallen.
I keep a bench-book of every building I've cut or mended. The mistakes are in red. There's a great deal of red. There is also a great deal of building.
When a shell breaks beyond mending, I'm called to prepare it for the Nursery. I hold the pieces together with my own fingers as it's carried. It isn't in my duties. It's in me.
I set a single amethyst shard into every window sill in the Nursery. It's useless. It catches the light. The young ones think it's magic, and I let them.
Did the old shellwrights know they were building the last great cities? Did they cut each block thinking: this is the final one? I cut mine as if it were.
A Chorrin once asked me to carve their name on a stone. I carved it small and low, where they'd only find it by kneeling. They knelt. They are still my friend.
I've never admitted this: the flawless joins in the old cities frighten me. They are the work of hands that did not doubt. Mine doubt on every cut. I think that's why mine stand.
You don't know how heavy a block is until you carry it for someone you love. I carried a column for my elder. It felt like carrying the whole Spire, and like no weight at all.
I test every stair by sitting on it, not walking. If a stair is happy to be sat on, it's happy to be walked. Don't stare. It's science.
{neighbour} brought me a cracked cup once. Not a shell, not a block: a cup. I mended it. It was the first time anyone brought me something small. It's still on my bench.
I've started building one thing a year with no purpose. Last year, a small arch behind the Nursery that leads nowhere. The year before, a bench for nobody. They're my favourites.
A good shellwright listens to the stone. A great one listens to the people standing around it. I'm trying, {player}. You're a surprisingly easy room to build for.
9: I'd like to make you something. A little lid for your door, so you have a bit of the Spire wherever you go.
When I close, my shell will be hard and plain and properly hinged. I've been checking it myself for years. Professional pride.
You've been knocked about, {player}. I can see it. I can't mend people without shells. I wish I could. Sit a while anyway.
I've never built anything that will last as long as the old cities. But I've built things people lived in. Lately that seems enough.
I'm cutting a door for you. No hinge, no lock, just a frame, to be hung somewhere in {village}. Walk through it whenever you like. It's the best way I know to say 'welcome'.
I carved your mark on the underside of the east bridge, where only a Driftray looking up would see it. A building should carry whoever it's grateful for.
When I close, set my shell at the foot of the stair I never finished. I left a step out on purpose. I wanted someone to know there was always room to add to it.
I'll tell you the secret of the courtesy-cut. Hold the chisel as you'd hold a small bird: not so loose it flies, not so tight it chokes. Same with a friend. Same with you.
There's a hollow in my bench where I sit to think. Yesterday I realised I'd carved it big enough for two. I can't explain it. Come and sit.
Everything I build will fall, in time. Everything. I've made my peace with that. But the afternoon you leaned on my rail and talked, I'd like to keep. I can't carve that. I'm trying.
I'm slow to say what I mean, so I'll say it in stone: every window I've cut this year is angled so the light lands where you stand. Don't check. Just stand there.
One block in the Spire is softer than the rest. A hand's weight of pale purpur I never could harden. I think of it as you: out of place, improving everything.
If the Court ever came, I would bring the roof down on their heads before they reached your door. I've measured the beams. It's the only violent thing I've ever planned. I'm quite proud of the sums.
I've mended many things, but I never learned to mend a day. I only learned to build a place where the good ones can sit down. You gave me the good ones.
I'm not good with words. Here's what I'll say: I would cut a whole new island for you, if the stone could be persuaded. It can't. So I cut a chair.

0: I fly Driftrays across the gaps between islands. Yes, over the void. No, I don't look down. Looking down is for the void.
The Roost is mine. A deck over a pier, open at the back so the rays can land. Don't stand on the open end. They don't look first.
Driftrays ride the void currents. You can't see them, but they're there, like the slope of a lid. A good {job} feels them through the ray.
Chorus flowers. That's how you tame a Driftray. Hold one out and be very, very patient. Then hold on.
A ray needs three things: a flower, a steady hand and a flight path. Two out of three won't do. I have tried.
Letters go in a satchel of void-cloth, sealed with a drop of resin, and addressed twice: once for the recipient, once for the ray, who has opinions.
I fly by the bell, not by any sky. Whatever the bell says, I am in the air.
The gaps between islands are named, like streets. Little Gap. The Long Dark. Mind the Quarrel, which is a gap named for an argument nobody remembers.
Offer a ray a flower on the flat of your palm, never on the fingers. Three thin fingers look like three small fish. I have stopped counting mine aloud.
Rays are patient, clever and mostly interested in sleeping. They are the best of us. I hope I'm half as calm when I am a shell.
I'm the {job} in {village}. The rota says I carry letters. The truth is I carry news, warnings, the occasional jar of chorus jelly from the Steads, and a great deal of nerve.
To land, I tilt the ray's wing. To rise, I flatten it. It's about as difficult as a door. The door is a hundred blocks up and made of nothing.
Every flight has a log. Every log begins the same way: 'Took off. Looked down. Did not.' I have decided that is the whole art.
The best saddle is a folded robe. The worst is the Archive's stool. I have learned both by sitting on them.
Rays fly crooked on a crossing current. The void has no wind, so I blame the rays. The rays blame me. It's a good partnership.
3: My ray is called Long Margin. Every wayfinder names their first ray after something in the Archive. Tradition. I resent it.
The other islands are farther than they look. Everything out here is. Distance is the void's only joke.
I carry letters between the Spires and the Steads. The Chorrin blink theirs across. Show-offs. Mine arrive in the right order.
If you see a glowing tail out over the void, that's a wayfinder coming home. Or a wild ray coming to see what you're eating.
The village called Halfshut is named for its Spire, which stands open to one gap and shut to the other. I land on the shut side. It's the polite one.
A ray called Ledger Slip once carried me three islands past my stop and back. I wasn't cross. It was the most interesting delivery I ever made.
The satchel has a pocket for apologies: late letters, wrong letters, letters written in the heat of the moment. I read none. I deliver them all with the same face.
Flying in the closed hours is the quietest thing there is. The rod-lamps below look like a second set of stars. I don't mind how far I might fall, since I'm already looking up.
If a ray refuses a flower, it isn't being rude; it's telling you that you chose the wrong flower. The Chorrin can read the signs. I can read the Chorrin. It's a chain.
I once delivered a letter to someone who had already closed. The family wrote back to thank me. It's the kindest reply I ever received.
At the edge of every island is a lamp for incoming rays. Not for the rays, who see in the dark. For the wayfinders, who can't. Mutual dependence, as ever.
A ray's tail tip glows brightest when it's content. When mine is sulking, I pretend I can't see it. Dignity matters in a partnership.
The hardest flight is the empty one. Satchel light, nothing to prove, and your mind fills the room. It's a very large room, out there.
There is a gap where the current turns and the ray goes quiet. I call it the Slow Door. I don't know what it opens onto. I always mean to ask.
The Chorrin send chorus fruit over by blinking. It arrives bruised. I fly it in a basket and it arrives perfect. They admit this is better. They do not admit it to my face.
6: I flew out to the old cities once. Saw the ships, saw the shells in the towers. Turned round. Didn't speak for a long while.
I fell once. My ray caught me a hundred blocks down. I don't remember screaming. The ray does; it's been nervous of me since.
Out over the gaps, nobody's watching. I sing. Badly. The rays don't mind. Please don't let it reach the Archive.
You fly too, don't you? Those wings you came in on. I've watched. You fly like someone who has never fallen. Lucky.
The first time I flew alone my ray stopped dead in the air and hovered. I was mortified. Then I looked around. We were exactly between two lamps, and the view was perfect. It knew.
I have mapped every gap from here to the third rim. The map is private. It has places on it that are not in the Archive. One or two aren't on any island.
I once carried a closing-notice. I flew very slowly. The recipient was waiting at the landing, lid already wide open. They knew from the way I flew.
When I fly past the old cities I keep to the outer edge and I make no sound. Not from fear. From manners. Though, honestly, a little from fear.
I fear one thing in the whole End, and it isn't the void. It's coming home to find the Roost empty: no rays, no lamp, nobody. It hasn't happened. I check anyway.
A ray taught me how to wait. At the top of a climb, you hold your breath and the ray holds the sky, and for a moment everything belongs to nobody. I'd like to show you.
I have a favourite gap. I won't say which. I go out there sometimes and simply float. I come back lighter, and no one knows where I have been, and no one asks.
People think a wayfinder knows the way. I don't. I know the way back. It's a different skill, and a far more useful one.
I carry more than letters, you know. I carry how a message sounded as it was written: the hurry in a hand, a tear dried on a fold. I am never lonely up there. I have everyone's feelings in a bag.
My first ray died old and calm in the Roost at the end of a lit span. I sat with them until the lamps dimmed. Then I took the next ray out and flew until I couldn't see.
The route to your side of the End is one I could fly blindfolded. Not a joke. I have done it. I'd tell you the names of the gaps, but you'd say they sound ridiculous. They do.
9: When I close, put my shell somewhere the rays fly past. I'd like to hear them, if the closed hear anything.
I'll fly you anywhere. Anywhere at all. That's not an offer I make. It's in the record that I don't.
Long Margin likes you. It has never liked anyone. I'm a little jealous, and a great deal relieved.
Some days I think of flying past the last island just to see. Then I think of who'd be left wondering. Lately, I think of you.
I've made a place on Long Margin's saddle for you, behind me. Sit tight and look at the stars and not at my robes, which flutter. It isn't dignified.
If I ever don't come back from a flight, search the third gap first. I always leave a lamp there. It's where I'd go to be found.
You gave me a reason to look down. Not into the void. At the island, the lit windows, the figures walking. Somebody down there is walking toward me. I like that.
I've renamed the last gap before home. It was called Nowhere Near. Now it is called {player}'s Crossing. It isn't official. The rays have already adopted it.
Long Margin sleeps by the window now, to see you coming. I have never known a ray to wait for anyone. It's embarrassing for us both.
If you ever want to go further than the lamps go, say so. I'll fly you past the last lit gap, to where the void lies like a still, blank page. We won't speak. That's the point.
I used to ask the old shells, in a way, for safe flights. Now I say your name instead. I don't think the shells mind. They would have liked you.
I've always loved leaving. It was the whole point of the job. Lately I like arriving even more, and I think it's because you might be there.
The End has no top. You could fly up for ever. I used to love that. Now it makes me want a roof with a window in it, and you underneath.
One day I shall write a log with no flight in it. Just: 'Stayed. Talked. Regretted nothing.' I'll file it under 'Wayfinders, Retirement Of'. It will be very thin.
When I close, read the log of my last flight aloud before the lamps. Make it a long one. Add a few extra gaps. I'd like to be remembered as having flown farther than I did.

0: I'm the Keeper of Shells. The young ones, whose lids pop open at everything, and the old shells, who don't open any more. The Nursery holds both.
Quietly, please. Half the Nursery is asleep and the other half is only pretending.
The nest by the wall is where the softest shells sleep. They harden slowly. Don't tap them. Everyone wants to tap them.
The shells by the door aren't empty. Not to us. I dust them every lit hour.
The Nursery has three rules: no sudden light, no sudden noise, no sudden questions. The young ones break all three before I've finished the sentence.
A soft shell must be turned once each lit span, so it doesn't harden flat on one side. I turn a dozen. By the bell my arms feel as old as the nest.
Young lids open at thirty wakings or so. Some at ten, some at ninety. It's never earlier when you are watching, and never later when you've just left the room.
I sing to the nest in a tuneless drone called the Counting. It lists every shell by name, oldest to newest. The oldest don't mind the repetition.
The cloth in the nest is changed at every bell. The soft shells like it warm, so I warm it by sitting on it first. It is the least dignified part of the work.
If you hold a young one, hold the whole shell, never the lid. The lid is the part that remembers being held wrong.
The naming-lamp is chosen weeks before a lid opens and lit the night it does. I choose the lamp and wait. Some nights I've chosen five.
I'm the {job} in {village}. I keep a ledger of firsts: first lid, first word, first gap crossed, first lie told. The last is always a delight.
Young ones fear three things: the dark, the Tower bell, and being the only open lid in a room of shut ones. I'm afraid of all three too, if I'm honest.
A soft shell is the colour of popped chorus. A hard shell is the colour of a bruise. The shades between are the loveliest sight in the Nursery. I'd paint them if I could.
Please don't give the young ones anything sweet. They glow from the inside afterwards and won't sleep. Last time the whole Nursery looked like the Lamp Court.
3: A young lid pops open at everything: a noise, a light, a Driftray, a word they don't know. It's exhausting. It's the best sound in {village}.
We name them the night their lid first opens. I've been at every naming in {village} for eighty years. I still weep. Lid down.
The old shells sit with the young ones. The young learn to be still. The old... well. We hope they hear the laughing.
I'm the {job}. Every closed shell here has a lamp beside it, and every lamp has my mark on the rota. Nobody is forgotten in {village}.
One young one refused to open for forty wakings. Wouldn't eat, wouldn't talk. Then someone dropped a ladle in the kitchen and they popped open to look. Never underestimate a ladle.
I tell the young ones a story each closed hour, the same one, with a single detail changed each night. The first to notice chooses the next detail. They think I'm a poor storyteller. I let them.
At a naming I trace the new lid for the record, and the new one adds a drawing of what they see through the gap. They're all of the same thing: a bright spot and a larger dark. Every single one.
When two shells quarrel I put them in the same nest and wait for the bell. By the second chime they're asleep against each other. The method is unscientific. It has never failed.
The old shells by the door have names too, carved on the lip of the nest. A young one will read one aloud now and then. Nobody tells them to. It's a small, cheerful grace.
I keep a feather in my sleeve for coaxing sleepy lids. When it works, the lid flips open and the first thing they see is me, bent double, beaming.
Ivory shells, the 'old shell' colour on a young one, are rare, and the village makes a fuss. I don't. Fuss makes them shy. Ivory is only a colour on the same frightened, hopeful heart.
In the Long Watch we hushed the Nursery with hangings of void-cloth, so no cry would reach the centre. I've taken down every one but one. That one I leave, in memory.
I check a young one's hinge after any fall. They fall a great deal. It's the one thing they do reliably.
Whisper something to a sleeping shell and in the lit hours they'll say it back to you. It's a Nursery secret and a terrible power. I've used it only for good, and twice for mischief.
The best moment in this work is at the end of a naming, when the new name is said aloud and the lid turns toward it. Always toward the sound. I have yet to get used to it.
6: Sometimes a shell I've kept since it was soft goes off to be a wayfinder, or an archivist. I'm proud. I also count the bells until they visit.
The hardest part isn't the young. It's sitting with someone as their lid closes the last time. I've done it many times. It doesn't get lighter.
The young ones talk about you. 'The Dragon one'. They act out your fight with chorus stalks. You lose, usually. They're working on it.
I keep a soft cloth in my sleeve for wiping young lids. I've used it on three elders, two archivists and once on myself. Don't ask.
I mind the soft shells because I was minded. I was a loud one, and my keeper was a patient one, and I have been trying to be the second ever since.
A young one asked me what comes after the last opening. I said: a lamp is lit. They said: and then? I said: someone sits with you. They said: always? I said: yes. Always.
A young one asked whether you were really as tall as the stories. I said you're as tall as you decide to be. They went away looking thoughtful. I hope I did no harm.
I've sat with eleven shells as they closed. Each had a different last thing to say. One asked whether the lamp was lit. It was. They seemed to relax.
I can't leave the Nursery for long. Not because it would fall apart. Because I would. A quiet room full of the sleeping is the only place I feel quite useful.
A soft shell fell asleep on my sleeve once, and I couldn't move for five bells. I counted the stitches. I know that sleeve better now than my own face.
I used to wish the young ones would grow faster. Now I want them small a little longer. Everyone does, by the end. It's the one thing you can't tell the young.
When the soft shells hear the Tower bell they all open at once, a ripple down the nest. It sounds like a page turning, if a page were the size of a room. It's why I stay.
I'm not allowed favourites. I have favourites. Please don't tell the small ones. They already suspect, and have started behaving suspiciously well.
There is a shell near the back, very old, closed before I was lit. I speak to it every waking. I've never had an answer. I'd be so alarmed if I did, and so very glad.
You are right to be gentle with the young. Their lids don't harden for a long time. I see you hold your hands loose around them. You learned that somewhere. I'd like to know where.
9: If anything happens to {village}, take the young ones first. The old shells will understand. They always did.
I think of you as one of mine, a little. You came to us new and loud and full of questions. That's how they all start.
When it's my turn to close, I want to be in the Nursery, near the nest. The noise will keep me company.
There's a soft shell in the nest whose lid opened the night you killed the Dragon. Every lamp flickered. We named them for that night. For you, really.
When the soft shells ask for a story, I tell them about you now. In the story you always arrive just in time with the right thing in your pocket. They never notice it's nearly true.
I've set a nest aside for you. Not for sleeping. For sitting. The warmest corner by the old shells. Everyone needs somewhere to stop and be the youngest.
I worried I'd run out of tenderness one day, after so many young ones. Then you came along and I found I had more.
Once, half asleep in the nest, I called you by a young one's name. You answered. You answered to it perfectly. I have never been so embarrassed or so happy.
The old shells by the door have been moved a little closer to your usual place. I know. They don't mind. I think they like the company. I know I do.
Stay a little soft, {player}. There are things I want to show you, and I'd like you to see them with your lid still half open, as it were.
When I close, I'd like the soft ones to hear a story in which I was a thing that was kind, and a bit late, and always carrying a cloth. And you are in it. Kindly. Obviously.
Some days the Nursery is quiet enough that I can hear my own shell ticking. It's an old sound, like a clock. I listen for you in it, and sometimes I think I hear you.
You never ask me to be anyone but a keeper. That's rarer than you'd think. Most people want me to be a story, a rule, or a lamp. You just want me.
I keep one soft cloth in my sleeve for you, for wiping your lid. You haven't got one. I know. I keep it anyway. It's the cloth I use when I'm happy.
If you ever feel too heavy, come and sit by the nest. The young ones won't ask. They'll open, one at a time, and look. It works. It always does.

0: I keep the Crossing Hall. Half of it. The tower half. The Chorrin keeper has the dome. We share the hearth and argue about the door.
Welcome to the Hall. Long tables for talking, a hearth for warming, and one rule: no lids slammed, no blinking indoors.
Shulkin and Chorrin both pass through here. My work is seeing that they leave on speaking terms. Most lit hours, I manage.
I'm the {job}. I keep the Hall's ledger; the Chorrin keeper keeps theirs as a song. We compare them every year. They never match.
Chorrin leave a stone at the door when they enter, a habit from the Steads. Shulkin leave a glance. We have agreed these are equivalent.
The long tables are cut to two heights, one for the glide and one for the stool. Guests sit where they sit. Nobody has ever eaten at the wrong table. Several have tried.
There's a guest-ledger by the door: name, island, purpose. Under 'purpose' the Chorrin hum 'hello' and I write it down. I've stopped objecting.
I'm the {job} in {village}. The Hall opens at the first bell and closes at the third, and between them I stand about being exactly as welcome as the hearth.
Quarrels are allowed at the tables and forbidden at the hearth. The hearth is neutral. Everyone looks at the fire, and it's hard to be angry at something so pleased to see you.
Don't sit on the bench with the green cushion. It's the dome keeper's. It has been the dome keeper's for forty years. They sit on it like an old stone.
I keep a rack of cups on the shelf. Shulkin cups have lids. Chorrin cups have knobs. The Old Accord was written between a lid and a knob.
The Hall lamp is lit at the first bell by the Shulkin keeper and turned down at the third by the Chorrin keeper. It has been this way since the Accord. Neither of us has ever been late.
The Hall smells of warm stone and popped chorus. In both our tongues the smell is called 'welcome'. In ours it is a long word. In theirs, a short hum.
Travellers from other Spires ask for the guest niche. It's the best in the Hall: dry, warm, the lamp turned just so. I give it to anyone who looks tired. Everyone looks tired by the third bell.
If you have a complaint, there's a slate by the door. Please write on it. We read it once a waking. It's mostly 'too loud' and 'too quiet', in the same hand.
3: My counterpart in the dome and I have shared this Hall for decades. We still haven't agreed whether the door opens in or out.
The hearth is shared. Officially. Unofficially, the Chorrin side is warmer. I've measured. They say it's the stone. I say it's the cushions.
When our peoples quarrel, it comes here first. I pour drinks. They hum. I write. By the closed hours, usually, someone has laughed.
Both halves of the double door open together, or neither does. That's the whole Accord in one hinge.
The Hall keeps a small shelf of left-behind things: a glove of the Chorrin kind, a half-filled ledger, a ribbon. Nobody collects them. I dust them. Perhaps they're waiting for us.
A Shulkin never raises their voice in the Hall. A Chorrin never lowers theirs. The result is a pleasant buzz at precisely the volume both peoples can bear.
Festivals are a negotiation. They want drums. We want silence. The compromise is a drum played very slowly, with pauses. It's better than either of us expected.
On the Night of Lamps and Blooms each guest brings one light and one flower to the Hall hearth. The pile is magnificent. By the closed hours it is pure chaos, and everyone is happy.
I asked the dome keeper to teach me a Chorrin song once. They hummed for an hour. At the end they asked whether I had it. I said: 'Hum, in the key of warm.' They wept. It was perfect.
Letters from the Court sometimes appear on the step, sealed in black wax. Nobody sees who leaves them. We read them together, both peoples, at the long table. Together is the only way to read them.
There's a game we play in the Hall called 'whose idea was it?' Both peoples guess who invented some everyday thing. The Shulkin always guess wrong. It's the best argument we ever have.
The hearthstone cracks. A shellwright mends it every tenth waking, and every tenth waking the dome keeper says it's in a better mood cracked.
I seat guests by what they carry: lamps by the hearth, letters by the door, quarrels in the middle. A well-seated Hall is a kind of quiet architecture.
A traveller from the third rim once spent six wakings in the guest niche without a word. On the seventh they asked for a chair and a pen, and wrote us a hymn. I hold it dear.
Don't ask me to choose between Shulkin and Chorrin in the Hall. It's like choosing between my two hands. I use both. I'd miss either. And one of them is always better at the dishes.
6: The Chorrin fear we look down on them. We fear they'll forget us. Both are a little true. I keep the Hall so both can be less true.
I saw the Hall full once: the night word came the Dragon was dead. Both peoples, every table. The Chorrin sang. We wrote it down. Then we sang too.
My counterpart over in the dome is the best friend I have. I've never said so. It would make the arguing awkward.
A hallkeeper must be neutral. I am. Mostly. I do slightly favour whoever brings the most chorus.
I never meant to be a hallkeeper. I was meant for the Archive. Then I held the door open for a Chorrin once, and I've been holding it ever since.
Sometimes I come in during the closed hours, when the Hall is empty, and sit in the middle of the floor. It echoes with everyone who has ever sat there. I feel very small and very busy.

After a bad quarrel, a Shulkin and a Chorrin once left in opposite directions, both in anger. They met at the far bridge, each coming back to apologise. I saw them from the window. I pretended not to.
The Hall is a small treaty. We've never signed it. We simply keep showing up. I think that's what treaties actually are.
I worry about the day neither side needs the Hall. If the Accord holds firm, there will be nothing to keep. I will be glad. I will also be unemployed.
I hold two opinions at once about almost everything. The Hall requires it. At home I find I can't stop. It makes me poor company for deciding what to eat.
When you sit at the long table, I count who has turned to look. It's always everybody, both peoples. Not hostile; curious. It's a gift, being the shared curiosity.
A Chorrin hummed a lullaby for my closed elder once, in the Hall. I'd never heard it. I've never forgotten it. I have asked since, and they say it was only for that night.
The hardest guests are not the loud ones. They are the polite ones with a grievance. They sit at the table for hours saying nothing. I pour. Sooner or later there's a flood.
The ledgers disagree. Mine says the Hall has welcomed three thousand guests. The dome's says one thousand, but each one very well. I've come to prefer theirs.
Hosts grow tired in a way nobody warns you about. You give your attention away in small pieces all day, and come to the end with only dregs. You, {player}, are the first guest who ever poured for me.
9: If the Court ever moves against us, this Hall is where both peoples will stand. I've made sure there's room for you at the table.
You belong to neither people and to both. That makes you the most Crossing thing in the Crossing. Your name is over a hook by the door.
When I close, give the keys to whoever argues best with the dome keeper. That's the real qualification.
I've seen bitterness between our peoples, and love. You're the first stranger both sides speak of the same way. Fondly. Don't spoil it.
There's a hook by the Hall door with a lamp on it and a small tag that says 'for {player}, when they come'. It has hung there for years. I change the lamp when it dims.
I told the dome keeper you're welcome in the Hall at any hour. The dome keeper said: 'Obviously.' In forty years it's the first time we have agreed immediately.
I used to watch the door for trouble. Now I watch it for you. The posture is the same. The heart is not.
When the Hall is full and loud and the hearth is roaring, I find myself looking for your shape at the back. Not to serve you. Just to check you are still in the room.
There is room for you at the long table, and room at the round one, and a small stool by the hearth that belongs to nobody. It is yours. It's the best seat in {village}.
I'll tell you the Hall's secret. It isn't the Accord. It's that every hour someone is waiting to be let in, and I'm the one who gets to say yes. I'd say it to anyone. I say it best to you.
My elder's last instruction was to keep the door unlocked. I have, for a hundred years. Nobody has stolen anything but one cushion, and that came back with an apology and a better cushion.
I have given up being neutral about you. Neutrality was fine when I had nothing to lose. Write it on the slate by the door, if you like: I am on your side.
When I'm gone, the Hall's best cup goes to whoever is hardest to offend and easiest to make laugh. By my count that's you and the dome keeper. Please decide between you who pours.
I'd like to be remembered for the doors I held open, not the rules I kept. Tell the young ones that. Or tell them nothing and simply hold the door.
You're the only guest who has ever stayed after the third bell to help me stack the cups. I didn't know I was lonely. I'm glad to have been shown.

0: Welcome to my stall. Everything is priced, recorded and fair. Two of those three are guaranteed.
I trade with the Steads mostly. Their chorus for our cloth and rods. The Accord was always a market, whatever the songs say.
You may browse. Browsing is free. Touching is a separate negotiation.
I'm the {job} on this side of the market. The stall with chorus on its roof is the Chorrin one. Their prices are friendlier. Their sums are not.
Weights are checked at the first bell and rechecked at the third. A fair scale is a small miracle. A fair trader is a larger one, and rarer.
My stock: rods, void-cloth offcuts, resin, pressed paper, and a jar of glow ink I'll sell only if you promise to use it for something nice.
Prices are chalked on the slate. The slate is always right. If you disagree, argue with the slate. It is very patient and has been rubbed out many times.
No credit. No theft. No gifts of unusual size. If you wish to give me something large, we'll call it a trade, and I will find something to give back.
I'm the {job} in {village}. I buy what we make, sell what we lack, and in between I watch what people do with their purpur. It is the most honest window into a person.
Don't touch the purpur pyramid in the corner. It's the sample I refuse to sell. I have priced it at an obscene sum, hoping nobody ever has that much.
Chorus from the Steads arrives in baskets, and the baskets go back empty. Empty baskets are the one thing the Chorrin never forget to return, and the one thing I cannot understand.
Three things about trading: know what you want, know what they want, and know the difference. Most disputes are the difference.
A haggle isn't a quarrel. It's a dance in which both partners pretend to leave. Do try it. You will be surprised how tempting it is to step on a foot.
Everything on my stall has passed through my hands, and any one of them might be the thing that lasts a hundred years. I don't know which. That's why I wrap them so carefully.
Receipts are written in triplicate: yours, mine and the Archive's. The third is the one that matters. It's also the one nobody reads.
3: I keep a ledger of every trade I've ever made. Want to see your column? It's longer than you'd think.
The Chorrin haggle loudly and then give you a discount for good company. We haggle quietly and give you a receipt. Both work.
What I'd give for something from the Overworld. Anything. Bring me a leaf and I'll make you rich. Well. Rich in purpur.
Honesty is the best policy. It's also the only one the Archive will let me keep.
The Chorrin trader and I have a game. They name a price, I name a worse one, and we meet in the middle, where we both feel cheated. That's how you know it's fair.
I keep one chip of purpur from every trade that surprised me. The jar is mostly empty. The ones in it are my best memories.
Sell in the lit hours, buy in the closed. The prices are the same, but the mood is different. A trader who knows the mood of the market knows more than one who knows the numbers.
I won't sell anything I haven't tried. That is why I own a very odd collection of hats, none of which suit a Shulkin.
People ask what the most valuable thing on my stall is. It's the lamp over it. Without it, nothing else shows what it is.
A good trade leaves both sides slightly short and slightly delighted. A great trade leaves both having learned something. I've had four great trades. Two were with the same Chorrin.
A green stone from the Overworld? Show me. No, not to buy. Just to look. I'd write it up with a drawing and put it on the slate as a rumour.
A stall isn't a counter. It's a promise with a roof. I have repaired the roof three times and the promise never.
Debts go in the ledger in red. Mine has a page of red I've been meaning to clear for sixty years. It belongs to a Chorrin who closed. I can't bring myself to strike it.
The rarest thing in a market is a quiet afternoon. I sell it by not selling anything. It's the best price I get.
Once a waking I give away one thing, unannounced, to whoever looks as if they need it: a scrap of cloth, a small rod. It's bad business. It's why I'm still happy.
6: Between us, your rates are better than anyone's. Don't thank me; it's an investment. You keep coming back alive.
My elder ran this stall through the Long Watch. Nobody bought anything for a century. They opened every lit hour anyway.
A stall is a little shell, if you think about it. Body, gap, lid. When I pull the awning down, I'm closed. Truly closed. It's restful.
I've traded with the Chorrin all my life and I still can't tell when they're bluffing. They hum the same. It's infuriating. I adore it.
I was a poor trader when I began. I gave things away and called it a discount. My elder said: 'You're not in the wrong trade. You're in the wrong century.' Then handed me the stall.
I have turned down a fortune twice. Once because it was dishonest. Once because it was boring. I'm prouder of the second.
Everyone thinks a trader is cold. We aren't. We're simply honest about the cost of warmth. Your friendship is the only account in my book I haven't priced.
When the Court's envoys came, they bought nothing, sold nothing, and asked for a count of our stock. I counted it three times. I have never been so careful with a sum.
Traders say the best goods are the ones that give you an excuse to talk. I have a drawerful of excuses. You've needed none.
Sometimes I think the stall is less a shop than a lamp. People gather, not for what's sold, but because it's lit.
I once lost a whole span's takings on a mistaken sum. My elder said: 'Good. Now you know the number you can lose.' Terrible advice. Excellent advice.
I trade in things, but what I truly deal in is trust. A lid that opens a little wider for you than for others. That's the currency. Mine is open to you at all hours.
I dream of a shop with no prices, where everyone takes what they need. Then I wake and remember I would have given you the whole stall by now.
Sometimes a Chorrin turns up with nothing but a hum. I give them a basket. They hum a little louder. It's the finest trade I ever make.
I keep a chair at the stall for the one customer who never buys a thing. They look, they say 'hm', they stay an hour. It's you. I price that hour very highly.
9: For you, no prices. Don't argue. I've already written 'gift' in the ledger, and you know I can't cross things out.
If you ever need to leave the End in a hurry, I've a pack ready. Rods, chorus, cloth. Enough for a while. Just in case.
I've more purpur than I'll ever need. What I wanted was someone to tell about the deals. Sit. Let me tell you about the great chorus glut.
The best trade I ever made was a cracked rod for an hour of your company. Terrible business. The best on my books.
I've kept a column in my ledger for you since the first day. It's headed 'owed'. I owe you more than I can list. I'm paying it off in tiny instalments of attention.
If I retire, I'm leaving you the stall's real treasure: the lamp, the slate and the small drawer of excuses. You've never needed an excuse. Take it anyway.
A trader's greatest fear is being cheated. Mine is that you will leave without letting me do you a good turn. I'm still waiting. Please. I'll find something.
I've started giving a discount to anyone who mentions your name. I don't announce it. It's all written down: 'Discount: {player}'. I've lost money steadily since.
Trading is only caring about what someone else needs and being honest about what it costs. By that measure you are the best trader I've met, and you have never sold a thing.
I sit at the stall after the third bell with the shutters half down and a lamp lit, in case you wander by. The lamp is a rod. It costs very little. It has never paid for itself more.
My elder's last advice was 'never mix love and ledgers'. I've done it for sixty years, with you, and the books balance. I think my elder was wrong. They'd be pleased to be.
I once bought the loneliest rod in the market out of pity and put it on the stall. It sold within the hour. All it needed was to be seen. I'm rather like that rod. You saw me.
The deals I'm proudest of aren't the profitable ones. They're the ones where someone walked away happier than they came. I have a great pile of those now, mostly with your face on top.
If the market burned, the Hall fell and the Archive went, I think I'd be fine so long as I had the ledger with your column in it. Odd, since it is full of numbers, and all I see is a name.
I'm giving you an unlimited tab at the stall. There are two conditions: you must never repay it, and you must keep coming by. I've written it in the ledger. In ink.
